questions.prompt: During college, Rosalina sees the oral surgeon because all 4 of her wisdom teeth are impacted, causing pain and swelling. If Rosalina starts off with a normal total number of teeth for an adult, how many teeth does she have left after her wisdom teeth are removed?

choices.explanation: Incorrect. 20 is the number of baby (primary) teeth, not adult teeth.
Incorrect. 24 would mean 8 teeth were removed, not 4.
Correct. An adult has 32 teeth, and removing 4 wisdom teeth leaves 28.
Incorrect. 32 is the full adult set before the wisdom teeth were taken out.
Incorrect. 36 is more than a normal adult has.

questions.note: A dental item printed in the Respiratory part of the exam; filed under Digestive here.
questions.advancedExplanation: The full permanent (secondary) dentition is 32 teeth: in each of the four quadrants, 2 incisors, 1 canine, 2 premolars, and 3 molars — 8 per quadrant × 4 = 32. The third molars are the wisdom teeth, one per quadrant, erupting around ages 17–25. Removing all four leaves 32 − 4 = 28. Two numbers on the answer list are deliberate near-misses drawn from real dental facts. Twenty (A) is the number of deciduous (primary/baby) teeth, which lack premolars and have only 2 molars per quadrant; a student who confuses the two dentitions lands there. Twenty-four (B) is 32 minus eight, the answer if you removed all the third and second molars. Thirty-two (D) is the untouched adult count, and thirty-six (E) is not an anatomical number at all. The clinical detail in the stem is accurate: third molars are the most commonly impacted teeth because the modern human jaw frequently lacks the retromolar space to accommodate them, so they erupt partially or at an angle against the second molar, trapping plaque and producing pericoronitis — the pain and swelling described.
questions.explanation:
The answer is 28 teeth. A full set of adult teeth has 32 teeth. In each quarter of the mouth there are 2 incisors, 1 canine, 2 premolars, and 3 molars, which is 8 teeth. 8 teeth x 4 quarters = 32 teeth.

Wisdom teeth are the third (last) molars, one in each quarter of the mouth. Removing all four leaves 32 - 4 = 28 teeth. The number 20 is how many baby teeth children have, and 32 is the adult total before removal.

Big idea: teeth are part of the digestive system because they break food into smaller pieces (mechanical digestion). Knowing the types and numbers of teeth is part of mouth anatomy.

questions.prompt: Which of the following statements are true regarding cementum? (Select all that apply.)

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Enamel is the hardest substance in the body. Cementum is much softer.
Correct. Cementum is softer than dentin (and enamel).
Correct. Cementum is a mineralized tissue that contains calcium, similar to bone.

choices.text: It is easily visible during a dental exam
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Cementum covers the root, which is hidden under the gums, so it is not easily seen.

choices.text: It is an anchor for periodontal ligament
choices.explanation: Correct. The periodontal ligament fibers attach to the cementum and hold the tooth in the jaw.

questions.note: A dental item printed in the Respiratory part of the exam; filed under Digestive here.
questions.advancedExplanation: Cementum is the thin, bone-like mineralized tissue covering the root of a tooth. The three statements that survive are B, C, and E. Hardness (A false, B true). The mineralized dental tissues rank in a fixed order: enamel > dentin > cementum. Enamel is about 96% hydroxyapatite by weight and is the hardest substance in the human body. Dentin is roughly 70% mineral. Cementum is the softest of the three at about 45–50% mineral, with the remainder collagen and water. So A is false and B is true — and note that the exam has worded these two as complementary halves of the same hardness fact, which is a useful internal check: getting one right should force the other. Composition (C true). Cementum's mineral phase is hydroxyapatite, Ca₁₀(PO₄)₆(OH)₂, so it unambiguously contains calcium. Any mineralized tissue in the body — bone, enamel, dentin, cementum — will. Visibility (D false). Cementum begins at the cementoenamel junction and covers the root, which sits in the alveolar socket and is normally concealed by the gingiva. During a routine dental exam you see enamel only. Cementum becomes visible or exposed only pathologically, when gingival recession or periodontal disease uncovers the root — a common cause of sensitivity, since exposed cementum wears away quickly and bares the dentinal tubules. Attachment (E true). This is cementum's functional reason for existing. The Sharpey's fibers of the periodontal ligament embed into cementum at one end and into alveolar bone at the other, suspending the tooth in its socket as a shock-absorbing gomphosis rather than fusing it rigidly to the jaw.
questions.explanation:
The correct statements are that cementum is softer than dentin, contains calcium, and anchors the periodontal ligament. A tooth has layers. Enamel is the hard outer covering of the crown (the part you see). Dentin is under the enamel. Cementum is a thin, bone-like layer that covers the root, below the gums.

Cementum is the softest of these hard layers: enamel is hardest, then dentin, then cementum. Like bone, it contains calcium minerals. Its main job is to hold the root in place: tiny fibers called the periodontal ligament connect the cementum to the jawbone. Because cementum is on the root and hidden by gums and bone, a dentist cannot easily see it.

Big idea: each layer of a tooth has a different hardness and job. Teeth help start digestion by chewing food.

questions.prompt: Which of the following segments of the alimentary canal is the longest?

choices.explanation: Incorrect. The esophagus is only about 25 cm long.
Incorrect. The duodenum is the shortest part of the small intestine, about 25 cm.
Incorrect. The jejunum is long (about 2.5 m) but shorter than the ileum.
Correct. The ileum is about 3.5 m long, the longest section.
Incorrect. The colon is wide but only about 1.5 m long.

questions.advancedExplanation: Approximate lengths in a living adult: esophagus 25 cm, duodenum 25 cm, jejunum ~2.5 m, ileum ~3.5 m, colon ~1.5 m. The ileum wins. The conventional teaching is that the small intestine distal to the duodenum divides roughly two-fifths jejunum and three-fifths ileum, which settles the only close comparison on the list. The intuitive trap is the colon. It is far wider than the small intestine, dominates the periphery of an abdominal radiograph, and is the structure most people picture as "the big intestine" — but width is not length, and at about 1.5 m it is less than half the ileum. "Large" and "small" intestine refer to luminal diameter, not to length; the small intestine is roughly four times longer. The length difference is functional. The ileum is long because absorption takes contact time and surface area, and it is where the last of the nutrients, plus the two substances absorbed nowhere else — vitamin B₁₂ (bound to intrinsic factor) and conjugated bile salts — are recovered. That specificity is why ileal resection or Crohn's disease of the terminal ileum causes B₁₂ deficiency and bile-salt malabsorption, while jejunal disease does not.
questions.explanation:
The answer is the ileum. The small intestine has three parts: the duodenum (about 25 cm), the jejunum (about 2.5 m), and the ileum (about 3.5 m). The ileum is the last and longest part.

The colon (large intestine) is wider, which is why it is called 'large', but it is shorter, only about 1.5 m long. The esophagus is about 25 cm long. So the ileum is the longest single section of the alimentary canal.

Big idea: 'large' and 'small' intestine describe how wide the tubes are, not how long they are. The long small intestine gives lots of surface for absorbing nutrients.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is not a major function of the salivary glands?

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Saliva does lubricate food, so this is a real function.
Incorrect. Salivary glands make mucus, so this is a real function.
Incorrect. Salivary amylase starts starch digestion in the mouth.
Correct. Saliva does not contain protein-digesting peptidases; protein digestion begins in the stomach.
Incorrect. Saliva contains IgA antibodies that help defend the mouth.

questions.advancedExplanation: Saliva begins carbohydrate and fat digestion but does no meaningful protein digestion. Protein digestion starts in the stomach, where parietal cell HCl both denatures protein and converts pepsinogen to pepsin; it continues in the small intestine with pancreatic trypsin, chymotrypsin, and carboxypeptidase, and finishes at the brush border with true peptidases. There is no significant peptidase or protease in saliva — a deliberate design point, since an active protease in the mouth would digest the oral mucosa. Everything else listed is real. Lubrication (A) and mucus (B) come from the mucous acini of the sublingual and submandibular glands, letting the bolus slide and allowing speech. Salivary amylase, or ptyalin (C), from the parotid gland cleaves α-1,4 glycosidic bonds in starch, beginning carbohydrate digestion in the mouth — it is inactivated by gastric acid, but works inside the bolus for a time after swallowing (this is why a cracker held in the mouth turns sweet). Secretory IgA (E) is the dominant immunoglobulin of mucosal surfaces and is actively transported into saliva, where it neutralizes pathogens before they are swallowed. Two further salivary functions not on the list are worth knowing: lingual lipase, secreted by von Ebner's glands on the tongue and the only lipase that matters in infants, and bicarbonate buffering plus calcium and phosphate supersaturation, which neutralizes acid and remineralizes enamel. The last is why chronic dry mouth (xerostomia) produces rampant dental caries.
questions.explanation:
The answer is 'produces peptidase'. Peptidases are enzymes that break down proteins. Saliva does not contain them. Protein digestion starts in the stomach, with the enzyme pepsin.

Saliva does several other jobs. It has water and mucus that moisten and lubricate food so it is easy to swallow. It has amylase, an enzyme that starts breaking down starch. It also has IgA antibodies, which help protect the mouth from germs.

Big idea: chemical digestion of different nutrients starts in different places. Starch starts in the mouth, protein starts in the stomach, and fat is mostly digested in the small intestine.

questions.prompt: Which anatomic structure is regarded as the point of division between the upper gastrointestinal (GI) tract and the lower GI tract?

choices.explanation: Incorrect. The ampulla of Vater is where bile and pancreatic juice enter the duodenum, not the upper/lower dividing point.
Incorrect. The duodenum has bends, but the official dividing landmark is the ligament of Treitz.
Incorrect. The superior mesenteric artery is a blood vessel that supplies the intestines, not the divider.
Incorrect. The pyloric sphincter is the valve between the stomach and duodenum, but the duodenum still counts as upper GI tract.
Correct. The ligament of Treitz marks where the upper GI tract ends and the lower GI tract begins.

questions.advancedExplanation: The ligament of Treitz — properly the suspensory muscle of the duodenum — is a fibromuscular band descending from the right crus of the diaphragm to the duodenojejunal flexure, holding that bend in place. By clinical convention, everything proximal to it is the upper GI tract and everything distal is the lower GI tract. The division is not arbitrary; it is defined by what you can reach and what it means when a patient bleeds. An upper endoscope can visualize to approximately this point, and a colonoscope works retrograde from the other end. Bleeding proximal to the ligament passes through the acid of the stomach and the length of the small intestine, so hemoglobin is degraded to hematin and the stool emerges black and tarry (melena); bleeding distal to it has less transit time and tends to appear as bright or dark red blood per rectum (hematochezia). Hematemesis, by definition, is upper GI bleeding. The ligament is also the embryologic boundary where the foregut becomes the midgut and the blood supply switches from the celiac trunk to the superior mesenteric artery. The distractors are all real duodenal landmarks chosen to be plausible. The ampulla of Vater (A) is where the common bile and pancreatic ducts enter the second part of the duodenum — an important landmark, but not the upper/lower divider. The superior mesenteric artery (C) does cross the third part of the duodenum, and compression there causes SMA syndrome, but it is a vessel, not a boundary. The pyloric sphincter (D) is the strongest distractor since it is a true anatomical gate — but it divides the stomach from the small intestine, both of which are upper GI. "Duodenal angle" (B) is not a standard term.
questions.explanation:
The answer is the ligament of Treitz. This is a band of tissue that holds up the bend where the duodenum turns into the jejunum. Doctors use it as the dividing line between the upper GI tract and the lower GI tract.

The upper GI tract is everything above this point: mouth, esophagus, stomach, and duodenum. The lower GI tract is everything after it: jejunum, ileum, and large intestine. This matters in medicine, for example to describe where bleeding is coming from.

Big idea: the digestive tract is one long tube, and landmarks along it help us name and describe its sections.

questions.prompt: Waluigi developed a bad case of abdominal bloating, flatulence (passing gas), abdominal cramps, and diarrhea. He has no other symptoms. An hour ago, he had consumed a glass of milk with dinner, followed by a pint of mint chocolate chip ice cream for dessert. He felt normal before and during dinner. Which of the following is the most likely cause for his symptoms?

choices.explanation: Correct. Not having enough lactase (a disaccharidase) means lactose from milk is not digested, causing gas, bloating, and diarrhea.
Incorrect. Celiac disease is a reaction to gluten (in wheat), not to milk.
Incorrect. Food poisoning usually causes vomiting and fever and is not tied to how much dairy he ate.
Incorrect. A parasite would not cause symptoms right after one dairy-heavy meal.
Incorrect. Crohn's disease is a long-term inflammatory disease with other symptoms like weight loss and pain over time.

questions.advancedExplanation: Lactose is a disaccharide of glucose and galactose. It cannot be absorbed intact; it must be hydrolyzed at the brush border by lactase, a disaccharidase. Most of the world's adults downregulate lactase after weaning (lactase non-persistence), so undigested lactose passes to the colon, where bacteria ferment it to hydrogen, methane, carbon dioxide, and short-chain fatty acids. The gas produces the bloating, flatulence, and cramping; the osmotic load produces the diarrhea. Four features of the stem converge on this diagnosis and exclude the alternatives. The timing — symptoms within about an hour of a lactose load — matches the transit time to the colon; food poisoning typically takes 6–48 hours (and 1–6 hours only for preformed toxins such as Staphylococcus aureus, which cause prominent vomiting). The exposure is specifically a double dose of lactose, milk plus a pint of ice cream, with no other implicated food. He felt normal before and during dinner, pinning onset to the dairy. "He has no other symptoms" is the most deliberate clue in the question: no fever, no vomiting, no blood in the stool, no weight loss. That single clause eliminates the inflammatory and infectious causes. Celiac disease (B) is an immune reaction to gluten, not lactose, and produces chronic symptoms with weight loss and sometimes dermatitis herpetiformis — not a one-hour reaction to ice cream. Food poisoning (C) would ordinarily bring fever, vomiting, or malaise and would not be so tightly keyed to dairy. A parasite (D) such as Giardia causes symptoms over days to weeks after contaminated water exposure. Crohn's disease (E) is a chronic transmural inflammation with fever, weight loss, and often perianal disease; a single acute episode after ice cream in an otherwise well person is not Crohn's. (Secondary lactase deficiency can follow intestinal injury from any of these, but the question asks for the most likely cause of this episode.)
questions.explanation:
The answer is a disaccharidase deficiency, which here means lactose intolerance. Milk and ice cream contain lactose, a sugar made of two smaller sugars joined together (a disaccharide). The enzyme lactase, made by the small intestine, splits lactose so it can be absorbed.

If someone does not make enough lactase, the lactose passes into the large intestine. Bacteria there eat it and make gas, causing bloating, gas, and cramps. The lactose also pulls water into the intestine, causing diarrhea. Waluigi felt fine until he had a lot of dairy, and his symptoms started soon after, which fits perfectly.

Big idea: digestion needs the right enzyme for each kind of food. When an enzyme is missing, that food is not absorbed and can cause symptoms.

questions.prompt: Which type of diarrhea is Waluigi most likely experiencing?

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Exudative diarrhea comes from inflamed, damaged intestinal walls, often with blood or pus.
Incorrect. Fatty diarrhea happens when fat is not absorbed. Waluigi's problem is milk sugar.
Incorrect. Functional diarrhea has no clear cause like a missing enzyme.
Correct. Undigested lactose pulls water into the intestine by osmosis.
Incorrect. Secretory diarrhea is when the intestine actively pumps out fluid, as with some infections.

questions.advancedExplanation: Osmotic diarrhea occurs when a poorly absorbed, osmotically active solute remains in the gut lumen and holds water there against absorption. Undigested lactose is exactly that solute: each lactose molecule that is not cleaved stays in the lumen, and the short-chain fatty acids produced when colonic bacteria ferment it add further osmotically active particles. Water follows down the osmotic gradient into the lumen, and the stool becomes loose and voluminous. The defining clinical feature of osmotic diarrhea — and the way to confirm the reasoning — is that it stops when the patient stops eating the offending substance. Remove the lactose and the osmotic driver disappears. It also produces a high stool osmotic gap (>125 mOsm/kg), because unmeasured solutes rather than electrolytes are doing the work. Other osmotic diarrheas follow the same logic: sorbitol and mannitol in sugar-free gum, lactulose, magnesium-containing laxatives, and polyethylene glycol bowel preps. Secretory diarrhea (E) is the main contrast: here the epithelium actively pumps ions, usually chloride, into the lumen, as when cholera toxin or a heat-labile E. coli toxin locks adenylyl cyclase on. It is typically watery, high-volume, has a low osmotic gap, and crucially persists during fasting. Exudative diarrhea (A) involves mucosal inflammation and ulceration with blood, pus, and mucus in the stool — inflammatory bowel disease or invasive infection — and the stem explicitly denies other symptoms. Fatty diarrhea (B), or steatorrhea, is malabsorption of fat from pancreatic insufficiency or bile salt deficiency, producing greasy, floating, foul stools; lactose is a carbohydrate. Functional diarrhea (C) is the chronic, no-structural-cause diarrhea of irritable bowel syndrome, not a discrete episode with an obvious trigger.
questions.explanation:
The answer is osmotic diarrhea. Osmosis is the movement of water toward places with more dissolved particles. Undigested lactose stays in the intestine and acts like a sponge, pulling water into the gut.

That extra water makes the stool watery. A key sign of osmotic diarrhea is that it stops when the person stops eating the food that causes it. Secretory diarrhea is when the gut lining actively pumps out fluid (for example from cholera toxin). Exudative diarrhea comes from an inflamed, damaged lining. Fatty diarrhea comes from fat not being absorbed.

Big idea: water follows dissolved particles. That is why unabsorbed sugars in the intestine cause watery diarrhea.

questions.prompt: Most of the GI tract contain smooth muscles, which are not under a person’s voluntary control, but rather, under control of the autonomic nervous system. On the other hand, striated muscles can be voluntarily controlled and are less commonly found in the GI tract. Where in the GI tract can you find striated muscles? (Select all that apply.)

choices.explanation: Correct. Chewing and tongue movements use skeletal (striated) muscle.
Correct. The upper part of the esophagus has skeletal muscle for swallowing.
Incorrect. The stomach wall is made of smooth muscle, which works automatically.
Incorrect. The gallbladder squeezes using smooth muscle.
Incorrect. The colon moves its contents with smooth muscle.
Correct. The external anal sphincter is skeletal muscle you control on purpose.

questions.advancedExplanation: Skeletal muscle appears in the GI tract precisely where conscious control is useful — at the two ends, where material enters and leaves — and nowhere in between, where reflex automaticity is better. Mouth (A): the tongue is entirely skeletal muscle (intrinsic muscles shaping it, extrinsic muscles moving it), as are the muscles of mastication and the buccinator of the cheek. Chewing and the voluntary initiation of a swallow are deliberate acts. Esophagus (B): the esophagus is the key item and the best discriminator on the question, because its muscle composition changes along its length. The upper third (including the upper esophageal sphincter, the cricopharyngeus) is skeletal muscle; the middle third is a transitional mix; the lower third is smooth muscle. This is why the oropharyngeal phase of swallowing is voluntary and consciously interruptible, while the esophageal phase, once begun, proceeds as an involuntary peristaltic reflex you cannot stop. Anus (F): the anal canal has two sphincters, and the distinction matters. The internal anal sphincter is smooth muscle under autonomic control and relaxes reflexively when the rectum distends; the external anal sphincter is skeletal muscle innervated by the pudendal nerve (S2–S4) and under voluntary control. Continence depends on that voluntary override. The stomach (C), gallbladder (D), and colon (E) are smooth muscle throughout, which is why gastric churning, gallbladder contraction, and colonic haustration and mass movements are all involuntary. Note the mild inconsistency the question creates with #39: the colon's muscle is smooth even though its taeniae coli are specialized longitudinal bands.
questions.explanation:
The answers are the mouth, the esophagus, and the anus. Striated (skeletal) muscle is the kind you can control on purpose. It is found at the two ends of the digestive tract, where we choose when to chew, swallow, or go to the bathroom.

The mouth has skeletal muscles for chewing and moving the tongue. The upper part of the esophagus has skeletal muscle for the start of swallowing (the lower part is smooth muscle). The anus has an outer ring of skeletal muscle, the external anal sphincter, which lets us hold in stool. The stomach, gallbladder, and colon use only smooth muscle, which works automatically.

Big idea: most of the digestive tract moves food by itself using smooth muscle (peristalsis). Voluntary control is only at the beginning and the end.

questions.prompt: Colorectal cancer is the second most common cause of cancer deaths in the USA (after lung cancer), responsible for over 52,000 deaths in the USA in 2022 alone. What testing methods can be used for colorectal cancer screening? (Select all that apply.)

choices.explanation: Correct. Colonoscopy looks directly inside the colon and can remove polyps.
Correct. CT colonography is an approved screening test that makes 3D images of the colon.
Incorrect. MRI is not a standard screening test for colorectal cancer.
Correct. Stool tests check for hidden blood or cancer DNA.
Incorrect. Ultrasound cannot see inside the colon well enough for screening.

questions.advancedExplanation: Colorectal cancer screening works because almost all of these cancers arise from adenomatous polyps over roughly 10 years, giving a long window in which a visible, removable precursor exists. Screening tests fall into two families: visual/structural exams that find polyps, and stool-based tests that find evidence of an existing cancer. Colonoscopy (A) is the reference standard. It visualizes the entire colon and rectum and is uniquely both diagnostic and therapeutic — polyps are removed during the same procedure, which is why colonoscopy reduces incidence and not merely mortality. A normal exam buys a 10-year interval. CT scan (B) qualifies in the specific form of CT colonography (virtual colonoscopy), an accepted screening modality in American Cancer Society and USPSTF guidelines, performed every 5 years. It uses thin-section CT with colonic insufflation to reconstruct the lumen, still requires bowel prep, and requires a follow-up colonoscopy if a lesion is found. Note that an ordinary abdominal CT is not a screening test — the option is defensible only because CT colonography exists. Stool-based tests (D) include the fecal immunochemical test (FIT, annually), high-sensitivity guaiac FOBT (annually), and multitarget stool DNA testing such as Cologuard (every 3 years), which combines FIT with assays for altered DNA shed by neoplastic cells. They are non-invasive and need no prep, but must be repeated frequently and require colonoscopy if positive. MRI (C) and ultrasound (E) are not screening tests. Both have genuine roles in colorectal cancer, which is why they are good distractors: pelvic MRI is the standard for staging rectal cancer and assessing the circumferential resection margin, and endorectal ultrasound stages early rectal tumors. But staging a known cancer in a symptomatic patient is a different task from screening an asymptomatic population, and neither can reliably detect small polyps throughout the colon.
questions.explanation:
The answers are colonoscopy, CT scan, and stool-based tests. Screening means checking healthy people for early signs of cancer before they feel sick. Colorectal cancer often starts as small growths called polyps, so finding and removing them early saves lives.

A colonoscopy uses a long camera to look inside the whole colon and can remove polyps. A special CT scan of the colon (CT colonography, or 'virtual colonoscopy') makes 3D pictures to find polyps. Stool tests look for hidden blood or cancer DNA in poop. MRI and ultrasound are not used for routine colorectal cancer screening.

Big idea: cancers of the digestive system are easier to treat when found early, so doctors use screening tests.

questions.prompt: Cirrhosis is late stage scarring of the liver which can lead to liver failure and death. It can be caused by a number of factors including alcohol abuse, hepatitis virus infection, or one of several hereditary conditions, among others. Which of the following cell types is most responsible for scarring of the liver?

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Hepatocytes are the main working cells of the liver. They get injured, but they do not make the scar tissue.
Incorrect. Cholangiocytes line the bile ducts. They are not the main scar-making cells.
Incorrect. Kupffer cells are immune cells that clean the blood. They release signals that wake up stellate cells, but they do not make the scar.
Correct. Activated stellate cells make the collagen that scars the liver.
Incorrect. Lymphocytes are immune cells; they can cause inflammation but do not make the scar tissue.

questions.advancedExplanation: Hepatic stellate cells — also called Ito cells, lipocytes, or perisinusoidal cells — reside in the space of Disse between the sinusoidal endothelium and the hepatocyte plates. In a healthy liver they are quiescent and their job is storage: they hold the body's main reserve of vitamin A as retinyl ester droplets, and they maintain normal extracellular matrix. Chronic injury of any kind changes that. Signals from damaged hepatocytes, activated Kupffer cells (TGF-β is the dominant one, with PDGF driving proliferation), and oxidative stress cause stellate cells to transdifferentiate into myofibroblast-like cells. They lose their retinoid droplets, acquire α-smooth muscle actin, become contractile and proliferative, and secrete large amounts of type I and III collagen into the space of Disse. The result is fibrosis: the sinusoids are "capillarized," the fenestrations that let plasma bathe hepatocytes are lost, exchange fails, and contractile stellate cells raise sinusoidal resistance — the beginning of portal hypertension. When collagen deposition organizes into bridging septa that surround regenerative nodules, the diagnosis is cirrhosis. The crucial insight the question tests is that the cell that dies is not the cell that scars. Hepatocytes (A) are the parenchymal workhorses and the usual victims of alcohol, virus, or iron, but they do not make the scar. Cholangiocytes (B) line bile ducts and are the targets in primary biliary cholangitis; they participate in the ductular reaction but are not the main collagen source. Kupffer cells (C) are the liver's resident macrophages and are genuinely important — they are the cells that release the TGF-β that activates stellate cells — making them the strongest distractor; but they are the signal, not the source of matrix. Lymphocytes (E) sustain the inflammation in viral and autoimmune hepatitis without producing collagen. Because stellate cell activation is in principle reversible, it is the central target of antifibrotic drug development, and fibrosis is now known to regress when the underlying injury — alcohol, hepatitis C — is removed.
questions.explanation:
The answer is stellate cells. Stellate cells sit in the liver and normally store vitamin A. When the liver is hurt again and again (for example by alcohol or hepatitis), these cells change and start making large amounts of collagen, the tough protein in scar tissue.

Over years, this scar tissue builds up and replaces healthy liver tissue. That is cirrhosis. Hepatocytes are the main working liver cells that get damaged, Kupffer cells are immune cells that clean the blood (they help trigger the stellate cells but do not make the scar themselves), and cholangiocytes line the bile ducts.

Big idea: the liver has several kinds of cells with different jobs. Long-term damage leads to scarring, which stops the liver from doing its jobs, including making bile for digestion.

questions.prompt: Which of these organs or structures in the GI tract can a human being survive without? Assume that the entire organ is removed, and that the person cannot receive a transplant. (Select all that apply.)

choices.explanation: Incorrect. The liver does hundreds of essential jobs, so a person cannot live without it (unless they get a transplant).
Correct. The gallbladder only stores bile. Many people have it removed and live normally.
Incorrect. The small intestine is where most nutrients are absorbed, so it is essential.
Correct. People can live without a colon by having the small intestine empty into an ostomy bag.
Incorrect. The mesentery holds the blood vessels that feed the intestines, so losing it all is not survivable.
Correct. The greater omentum is a fatty apron that can be removed safely.

questions.advancedExplanation: Gallbladder (B). The gallbladder stores and concentrates bile; it does not make it. After cholecystectomy — one of the most common abdominal operations performed — the liver continues producing bile, which simply drains continuously into the duodenum rather than in a postprandial bolus. Most people are entirely asymptomatic; some have loose stools or trouble with very fatty meals until the bile ducts dilate and adapt. Colon (D). The colon's jobs are water and electrolyte reclamation, storage, and housing the microbiota. Total colectomy is routinely performed for ulcerative colitis and familial adenomatous polyposis, with either an end ileostomy or an ileal pouch–anal anastomosis. The small intestine adapts and increases its own water absorption. Patients live normal lifespans with looser, more frequent stools. Greater omentum (F). This fatty apron hanging from the greater curvature of the stomach is an immune and repair organ — the "abdominal policeman" that migrates to wall off inflammation, and a site of milky-spot lymphoid tissue. It is removed routinely as part of a radical gastrectomy (omentectomy) for gastric cancer and in ovarian cancer debulking, with no essential loss of function. Liver (A) — no. The liver has no functional substitute and no mechanical bypass. It synthesizes albumin and all the clotting factors except von Willebrand factor, converts ammonia to urea, metabolizes drugs and hormones, conjugates bilirubin, stores glycogen, and produces bile. Total hepatectomy without transplant is fatal within hours to days from hypoglycemia, coagulopathy, and hyperammonemic encephalopathy. The stem's "cannot receive a transplant" clause is what makes this definitive. Small intestine (C) — no. Essentially all nutrient absorption happens here. Total enterectomy produces short bowel syndrome in its most extreme form; survival would depend on lifelong total parenteral nutrition, which is a replacement therapy rather than survival without the organ, and which eventually fails through line sepsis and TPN-associated liver disease. Mesentery (E) — no, and this is the question's real discriminator. The mesentery looks like inert connective tissue, but it is the conduit: the superior and inferior mesenteric arteries and veins, the lymphatics draining to the cisterna chyli, and the autonomic nerves all travel within it to reach the bowel. Removing the entire mesentery devascularizes the entire intestine, which infarcts. Separating "a structure the gut can live without" from "the structure that carries the gut's blood supply" is exactly what the option is probing.
questions.explanation:
The answers are the gallbladder, the colon, and the greater omentum. People can live a normal life without these, because other organs can take over their jobs or their jobs are not essential.

The gallbladder only stores bile; without it, bile drips straight from the liver into the intestine. Without a colon, a person can live by having the small intestine empty into a bag (an ileostomy). The greater omentum is a fatty apron in the belly that can be removed. But nobody can live without a liver, and losing the whole small intestine or the mesentery (which carries its blood vessels) means the body cannot absorb food.

Big idea: some organs are essential and some are helpers. The liver and small intestine are essential; storage and support structures can often be removed.

questions.prompt: Which of these hormones or neurotransmitters does NOT promote gastric acid secretion? (Select all that apply.)

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Acetylcholine from the vagus nerve stimulates parietal cells to make acid.
Correct. Epinephrine is a fight-or-flight hormone that slows digestion; it does not promote acid secretion.
Incorrect. Histamine strongly stimulates parietal cells to make acid (that is why acid-reducing drugs block histamine).
Incorrect. Gastrin is the main hormone that stimulates acid secretion.
Correct. Secretin reduces stomach acid and tells the pancreas to release bicarbonate.

questions.advancedExplanation: Gastric parietal cells are driven by exactly three stimulatory ligands, each with its own receptor, converging on the H⁺/K⁺-ATPase proton pump: acetylcholine (A) from vagal fibers acting on M3 muscarinic receptors; gastrin (D) from antral G cells acting on CCK-B receptors; and histamine (C) from enterochromaffin-like (ECL) cells acting on H2 receptors. Histamine is the central amplifier — ACh and gastrin both also stimulate ECL cells to release histamine — which is why H2 blockers such as ranitidine and famotidine suppress acid from all three pathways at once. Secretin (E) is the clearest inhibitor on the list and was, historically, the first hormone ever described (Bayliss and Starling, 1902). It is released by S cells of the duodenum when acidic chyme arrives, and its purpose is to shut acid delivery down and neutralize what has already arrived: it stimulates pancreatic and biliary bicarbonate secretion, and it directly inhibits gastrin release and gastric acid secretion. It is a classic negative-feedback brake. Epinephrine (B) is the intended answer on the basis that the sympathetic nervous system opposes digestion. In "fight or flight," blood is diverted away from the splanchnic bed, GI motility and secretion are suppressed, and the three acid secretagogues above — all parasympathetic or enteric-hormonal — are not among them. Acid secretion is a vagal, "rest and digest" function. Nuance worth knowing. Choice B is a reasonable but not airtight item. There is experimental evidence that catecholamines can stimulate parietal cells through β-receptors, and acute stress raises acid output in some settings. At the Division B level, though, the intended framework is "ACh, gastrin, histamine stimulate; secretin and somatostatin inhibit; sympathetic activity suppresses digestion," under which B and E are correct. Somatostatin, prostaglandins, GIP, and CCK are the other physiologic inhibitors.
questions.explanation:
The answers are epinephrine and secretin. The question asks which chemicals do NOT turn on stomach acid. Three chemicals work together to turn acid on: acetylcholine (released by the vagus nerve when you see, smell, or taste food), gastrin (a hormone made by G cells in the stomach), and histamine (released by cells in the stomach lining). All three act on parietal cells, the cells that make hydrochloric acid.

Secretin does the opposite. When acidic food enters the duodenum, the duodenum releases secretin, which tells the stomach to make less acid and tells the pancreas to send bicarbonate to neutralize the acid. Epinephrine is the 'fight or flight' hormone; during stress, digestion slows down, so it does not promote acid.

Big idea: the stomach's acid is controlled by nerves and hormones. Some signals turn acid on (rest and digest, food in the stomach) and others turn it off (food reaching the intestine, stress).

questions.prompt: Which of the following products of the pancreas is involved in its endocrine function? (Select all that apply.)

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Amylase digests starch and is sent to the intestine, which is an exocrine job.
Correct. Glucagon is a hormone released into the blood to raise blood sugar, an endocrine job.
Correct. Insulin is a hormone released into the blood to lower blood sugar, an endocrine job.
Incorrect. Lipase digests fat in the intestine, an exocrine job.
Incorrect. Trypsinogen is an inactive protein-digesting enzyme sent to the intestine, an exocrine job.

questions.note: On the printed exam the options were lettered a, b, c, a, b (two "b" options); they are relabelled A-E here. The intended answer is glucagon and insulin.
questions.advancedExplanation: The pancreas is a dual-function gland. Its exocrine portion — about 98–99% of the gland by mass, organized into acini draining through a duct system — secretes digestive enzymes into the duodenum. Its endocrine portion, the scattered islets of Langerhans, secretes hormones directly into the bloodstream. The distinction the question tests is simply duct versus blood. Glucagon comes from islet alpha cells (about 20% of islet mass) and raises blood glucose through hepatic glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis. Insulin comes from islet beta cells (about 70%) and lowers blood glucose by driving uptake into muscle and adipose tissue via GLUT4 and promoting glycogen, protein, and fat synthesis. Both enter the portal blood, so both are endocrine. (The islets also produce somatostatin from delta cells and pancreatic polypeptide from PP cells.) The three exocrine products are amylase, which cleaves starch; lipase, which with colipase and bile salts hydrolyzes triglycerides and is the only significant fat-digesting enzyme in adults; and trypsinogen, the inactive zymogen of trypsin. Trypsinogen's inactivity is itself a protective design: it is activated only in the duodenum by brush-border enteropeptidase, after which trypsin activates the remaining zymogens. Premature intrapancreatic activation is the central event in acute pancreatitis, and hereditary pancreatitis is caused by PRSS1 mutations that make trypsinogen activate too easily. Flagged — exam formatting defect. The five options on the printed exam are lettered a. Amylase · b. Glucagon · c. Insulin · a. Lipase · b. Trypsinogen — the list restarts at "a" after the third item, so the letters a and b each appear twice. The official key's answer of "B, C" is therefore literally ambiguous: "B" could mean Glucagon or Trypsinogen. Any student who wrote the answers by letter rather than by name is at risk, and any student who selected the fourth and fifth options cannot be unambiguously graded. Recommended handling: accept any response that identifies glucagon and insulin by name or position, and treat letter-based answers charitably.
questions.explanation:
The answers are glucagon and insulin. The pancreas has two kinds of jobs. Its exocrine job is to make digestive juices that flow through a duct into the small intestine. Its endocrine job is to make hormones that go straight into the blood.

Small clusters of cells in the pancreas, called the islets of Langerhans, make the hormones insulin (lowers blood sugar) and glucagon (raises blood sugar). Amylase, lipase, and trypsinogen are digestive enzymes, so they belong to the exocrine job. (On the printed exam the choices were lettered a, b, c, a, b, so they are relabeled here.)

Big idea: 'endocrine' means hormones released into the blood, and 'exocrine' means secretions sent through a duct. The pancreas does both, which is why it matters for digestion and for blood sugar.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is NOT a function of the liver?

choices.explanation: Incorrect. The liver makes complement proteins and clotting factors.
Incorrect. The liver stores glucose as glycogen.
Incorrect. The liver removes toxins from the blood.

choices.text: Stores bile for use in fat digestion
choices.explanation: Correct. The liver makes bile, but the gallbladder stores it.

choices.text: Clears breakdown products of red blood cells
choices.explanation: Incorrect. The liver clears bilirubin, which comes from old red blood cells.

questions.advancedExplanation: The liver produces bile; the gallbladder stores and concentrates it. Hepatocytes continuously secrete roughly 600–1000 ml of bile per day into the canaliculi. Between meals the sphincter of Oddi is closed, so bile backs up the cystic duct into the gallbladder, which concentrates it five-to tenfold by reabsorbing water and electrolytes. When fat and protein reach the duodenum, CCK from I cells contracts the gallbladder and relaxes the sphincter of Oddi, delivering the concentrated bolus. The verb in the option — "stores" — is the entire trick, and it is a one-word distinction. The other four are genuine liver functions. A: the liver synthesizes nearly all plasma proteins, including albumin, complement components C3 and C5, and all clotting factors except factor VIII/vWF — which is why liver failure causes a prolonged prothrombin time and why INR is part of the MELD score. B: glycogenesis stores glucose as glycogen postprandially, and glycogenolysis plus gluconeogenesis releases it during fasting, making the liver the principal buffer of blood glucose. C: phase I (cytochrome P450 oxidation) and phase II (glucuronidation, sulfation, conjugation) reactions detoxify drugs, alcohol, and endogenous toxins, and the urea cycle converts ammonia to urea. E: Kupffer cells phagocytose senescent erythrocytes, heme is degraded to unconjugated bilirubin, hepatocytes conjugate it with glucuronic acid, and it is excreted in bile — failure at any step in this pathway produces jaundice.
questions.explanation:
The answer is 'stores bile for use in fat digestion'. The liver MAKES bile, but it does not store it. The gallbladder is the organ that stores and concentrates bile, then squeezes it into the small intestine when fatty food arrives.

The liver does all the other jobs listed. It makes blood-clotting proteins and complement proteins (part of the immune system). It stores extra glucose as glycogen for later. It removes toxins, alcohol, and drugs from the blood. It also breaks down hemoglobin from old red blood cells into bilirubin and gets rid of it in bile.

Big idea: the liver is like the body's chemical factory and cleaning station, while the gallbladder is just a storage bag for the bile the liver makes.

questions.prompt: Donkey Kong is so busy tossing barrels at Mario all day to keep him from saving the princess, that he had no time to eat at all. He is famished. Which of these hormones is most responsible for Donkey Kong’s hunger?

choices.explanation: Correct. Ghrelin from an empty stomach makes you feel hungry.
Incorrect. Leptin from fat cells reduces hunger.
Incorrect. Gastrin stimulates stomach acid, not hunger.
Incorrect. Motilin causes the stomach and intestine to squeeze between meals, but it is not the main hunger hormone.
Incorrect. Secretin tells the pancreas to release bicarbonate; it does not cause hunger.

questions.advancedExplanation: Ghrelin is the body's only known circulating orexigenic (appetite-stimulating) hormone, produced mainly by P/D1 cells in the fundus of an empty stomach. Its levels rise steeply before an anticipated meal and fall within an hour of eating. It acts on GHS-R receptors on neuropeptide Y / agouti-related peptide neurons in the arcuate nucleus of the hypothalamus, which drive food-seeking behavior and simultaneously inhibit the anorexigenic POMC neurons. The nickname is "the hunger hormone." Leptin (B) is ghrelin's counterpart and the most instructive wrong answer. Secreted by adipocytes in proportion to fat mass, it suppresses appetite by activating POMC neurons and inhibiting NPY/AgRP neurons — it is the long-term adiposity signal, where ghrelin is the short-term meal-timing signal. Selecting leptin means inverting the pair. Gastrin (C) drives gastric acid secretion from antral G cells but has no appetite role. Secretin (E) is a duodenal inhibitor of acid and stimulator of pancreatic bicarbonate (see #34). Motilin (D) is the trap that pairs with the following question: it is also released during fasting, but it produces the mechanical consequence of an empty gut rather than the sensation of hunger. A clinically telling detail: sleeve gastrectomy removes the gastric fundus, and the resulting drop in ghrelin is thought to contribute to the appetite suppression and weight loss that follow — evidence that ghrelin is causal rather than merely correlated with hunger.
questions.explanation:
The answer is ghrelin, often called the 'hunger hormone'. When your stomach has been empty for a while, cells in the stomach release ghrelin. It travels to the brain and makes you feel hungry.

Ghrelin levels are highest right before meals and drop after you eat. Leptin does the opposite: it is made by fat cells and tells the brain you have enough energy stored, which lowers hunger. Gastrin and secretin control stomach acid and digestion, not hunger.

Big idea: the digestive system talks to the brain using hormones. Ghrelin says 'eat', and leptin says 'you have enough'.

questions.prompt: Donkey Kong is so hungry that his abdomen starts to growl loudly. Which of these hormones is most responsible for this growling?

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Ghrelin makes you feel hungry, but motilin is the hormone that starts the squeezing waves that cause growling.
Incorrect. Leptin reduces hunger and has nothing to do with growling.
Incorrect. Gastrin mainly increases stomach acid when food arrives.
Correct. Motilin triggers the strong squeezing waves of the empty gut that cause growling.
Incorrect. Secretin controls bicarbonate release after a meal, not gut movement between meals.

questions.advancedExplanation: The growling is borborygmi, and it is a mechanical event, not an emotional one: it is the sound of gas and fluid being propelled through a largely empty gut, where there is no food to muffle the noise. The propulsion is produced by the migrating motor complex (MMC), a cyclical pattern of strong peristaltic contractions that sweeps from the stomach through the small intestine roughly every 90–120 minutes during fasting. Its function is housekeeping — clearing residual debris, mucus, desquamated cells, and bacteria toward the colon, which is also why MMC failure predisposes to small intestinal bacterial overgrowth. Motilin, secreted by M cells of the duodenal and jejunal mucosa in the interdigestive state, is the hormone that initiates phase III of the MMC, the burst of intense contractions responsible for the audible growling. Feeding abolishes the MMC and the sound stops. This question and #37 are deliberately paired, and both have the same five options so you must distinguish them precisely. Both ghrelin and motilin rise in the empty stomach — they are even structurally related peptides with homologous receptors — but ghrelin produces the sensation of hunger and motilin produces the contractions that make the noise. Choosing ghrelin here is the single most common error, because "hungry stomach growls" collapses the two into one. Note also that the macrolide antibiotic erythromycin is a motilin receptor agonist, which is why it is used off-label as a prokinetic in gastroparesis.
questions.explanation:
The answer is motilin. Between meals, the stomach and small intestine do strong waves of squeezing every 90 minutes or so. These waves sweep leftover food and bacteria along, like a housekeeper. Motilin, a hormone from the small intestine, starts these waves.

When the gut is nearly empty, these squeezing waves push gas and fluid around, which makes the growling sound (called borborygmi). Ghrelin makes you feel hungry and can boost these waves, but motilin is the main hormone that triggers them.

Big idea: the digestive tract keeps moving even when it is empty. Hormones control both when we feel hungry and how the gut moves.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is NOT a characteristic of the colon?

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Absorbing water is one of the colon's main jobs.
Incorrect. Haustra are the pouches that give the colon its segmented look.
Correct. Plicae circulares are folds in the small intestine, not the colon.
Incorrect. The colon houses most of the body's gut bacteria.
Incorrect. Bacteria living in the colon make vitamin K.

questions.advancedExplanation: Plicae circulares, also called the valves of Kerckring, are permanent circular folds of mucosa and submucosa that project into the lumen of the small intestine. They are most prominent in the distal duodenum and jejunum, diminish through the ileum, and are absent from the colon. Together with villi and microvilli they are one of the three tiers of surface-area amplification that take the small intestine from a bare tube of ~0.4 m² to roughly 200 m²; they also set the chyme spiraling to slow transit and improve contact with the absorptive epithelium. The colon needs none of that, because it absorbs water and electrolytes rather than nutrients, and its mucosa is flat, villus-free, and packed with goblet cells. Radiologically and endoscopically the distinction is practical: small bowel folds (valvulae conniventes) traverse the entire lumen, while colonic haustral folds do not — this is how a plain film distinguishes small bowel from large bowel obstruction. The other four are genuine colonic features. A: it reabsorbs 1–1.5 L of water per day, concentrating ~1500 ml of ileal effluent down to ~150 ml of stool. B: haustra are the characteristic sacculations produced by the taeniae coli — three longitudinal muscle bands shorter than the colon itself, which gather it into pouches. D: it houses roughly 10¹⁴ bacteria, the densest microbial community in the body. E: colonic bacteria synthesize vitamin K (menaquinone) and several B vitamins, which are then absorbed — technically the flora produce it rather than the colon itself, but this is standard phrasing, and it explains why prolonged broad-spectrum antibiotics can prolong the prothrombin time.
questions.explanation:
The answer is 'contains plicae circulares'. Plicae circulares are circular folds in the lining of the small intestine. They give the small intestine more surface area for absorbing nutrients. The colon does not have them.

The colon does everything else listed. It absorbs water and salts to turn liquid waste into solid stool. It has pouches called haustra that give it a bumpy look. It is home to trillions of helpful bacteria (gut flora), and those bacteria make vitamin K.

Big idea: the small and large intestines have different jobs, so they look different inside. The small intestine is built for absorbing nutrients; the large intestine is built for absorbing water and housing bacteria.

questions.prompt: Which of these viral infections of the liver is a top cause of cirrhosis and liver failure in the United States?

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Hepatitis A causes a short illness and does not become chronic.
Incorrect. Hepatitis B can cause cirrhosis, but in the United States hepatitis C is the bigger cause.
Correct. Chronic hepatitis C is a top cause of cirrhosis and liver failure in the US.
Incorrect. Hepatitis D only happens alongside hepatitis B and is rare in the US.
Incorrect. Hepatitis E is usually a short illness spread by contaminated water.

questions.advancedExplanation: Hepatitis C virus is an RNA flavivirus transmitted percutaneously — injection drug use today, transfusion before 1992 screening. Its defining feature is the one that makes it the answer: roughly 75–85% of acute infections become chronic. HCV is an RNA virus with no proofreading polymerase, so it mutates into a swarm of quasispecies faster than the immune system can clear it, and the acute infection is usually asymptomatic, so it goes undetected for decades. Of those chronically infected, 10–20% develop cirrhosis over 20–30 years, and cirrhotic patients then carry a 1–5% annual risk of hepatocellular carcinoma. HCV was for many years the leading indication for liver transplantation in the United States, and the CDC recommends one-time screening of all adults for this reason. Hepatitis B (B) is the strongest distractor and is the dominant cause of cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma worldwide, particularly in East Asia and sub-Saharan Africa where perinatal transmission is common and chronicity rates reach 90% in infants. But in adults it becomes chronic only about 5% of the time, and universal U.S. infant vaccination since 1991 has sharply limited its burden here. The question's "in the United States" is doing deliberate work. Hepatitis A (A) and hepatitis E (E) are fecal–orally transmitted, cause acute self-limited hepatitis, and essentially never become chronic in immunocompetent people — no chronicity, no cirrhosis. (HEV can chronify in transplant recipients, and is dangerous in pregnancy, but neither is the U.S. cirrhosis story.) Hepatitis D (D) is a defective satellite virus requiring HBsAg to assemble, so it can only infect someone who already has hepatitis B; co-infection accelerates progression but is uncommon in the U.S. A current footnote: direct-acting antivirals now cure over 95% of HCV infections in 8–12 weeks, so HCV's contribution is falling, and alcohol-associated liver disease and MASLD/NAFLD have overtaken it as leading causes of cirrhosis overall. Among viral causes, HCV remains the answer.
questions.explanation:
The answer is hepatitis C. Hepatitis means inflammation of the liver, and several viruses can cause it. Hepatitis C spreads mainly through blood, such as shared needles. Most people infected with it develop a long-lasting (chronic) infection, often without symptoms for years.

Over decades, chronic hepatitis C scars the liver (cirrhosis) and can lead to liver failure and liver cancer. In the United States it has been a leading cause of liver transplants. Hepatitis A and E usually cause short illnesses that go away. Hepatitis B can become chronic too, but in the US it causes fewer cases of cirrhosis than hepatitis C. Hepatitis D only infects people who already have hepatitis B.

Big idea: hepatitis is one of the digestive diseases you need to know. The different hepatitis viruses spread in different ways and cause different amounts of long-term damage.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is a correct order for the normal passage of contents through the alimentary canal?

choices.text: Jejunum, Cecum, Transverse colon, Sigmoid colon, Rectum
choices.explanation: Correct. Jejunum, cecum, transverse colon, sigmoid colon, and rectum are all in the correct order.

choices.text: Ileum, Duodenum, Cecum, Ascending colon, Rectum
choices.explanation: Incorrect. The duodenum comes before the ileum, not after it.

choices.text: Cecum, Duodenum, Ileum, Ascending colon, Descending colon
choices.explanation: Incorrect. The cecum comes after the small intestine, not before the duodenum.

choices.text: Duodenum, Ileum, Ascending colon, Cecum, Sigmoid colon
choices.explanation: Incorrect. The cecum comes before the ascending colon, not after it.

choices.text: Ileum, Jejunum, Cecum, Transverse colon, Rectum
choices.explanation: Incorrect. The jejunum comes before the ileum, not after it.

questions.advancedExplanation: The full sequence is: mouth → pharynx → esophagus → stomach →duodenum → jejunum → ileum→ ileocecal valve →cecum → ascending colon → transverse colon → descending colon → sigmoid colon → rectum→ anal canal. The critical reading skill here is that the options list subsets, not consecutive segments. A sequence is correct if the listed structures appear in the right relative order, even with gaps. Option A skips the ileum between jejunum and cecum, and skips ascending and descending colon — but jejunum does precede cecum, cecum does precede transverse colon, transverse does precede sigmoid, and sigmoid does precede rectum. The order holds. Each wrong option contains at least one true reversal. B puts the ileum before the duodenum, inverting the small intestine. C puts the cecum before the duodenum, which inverts large and small intestine, and also places the ascending colon after the cecum correctly but too late to rescue it. D places the ascending colon before the cecum, inverting the very first two segments of the large intestine — the cecum is the blind pouch the ileum empties into, and the ascending colon rises from it. E puts the ileum before the jejunum, which is the most frequently confused pair on the list. A quick strategy: scan each option for any pair you are certain about — duodenum before ileum, cecum before ascending colon, jejunum before ileum — and eliminate on the first violation. Only one option survives.
questions.explanation:
The answer is A: jejunum, cecum, transverse colon, sigmoid colon, rectum. The correct full path of food is: duodenum, jejunum, ileum, cecum, ascending colon, transverse colon, descending colon, sigmoid colon, rectum, anus. Choice A skips some steps, but every part it lists is in the right order.

Each other choice has at least one part out of order. For example, the ileum comes after the duodenum (not before), the cecum comes after the ileum (not before the duodenum), and the cecum comes before the ascending colon.

Big idea: the alimentary canal is one long tube, and food always moves through its parts in the same order. Memorizing that order is a basic part of digestive anatomy.

questions.prompt: What is the strongest known risk factor in the world for the development of stomach (gastric) cancer?
questions.answer: Helicobacter pylori infection of the stomach
questions.advancedExplanation: Helicobacter pylori is a Gram-negative, spiral, flagellated bacterium that colonizes the gastric mucus layer. It survives the stomach's acid by producing large amounts of urease, which hydrolyzes urea into ammonia and carbon dioxide and surrounds the organism in an alkaline cloud — the same reaction exploited by the urea breath test and the rapid urease (CLO) test used for diagnosis. It infects roughly half the world's population, with much higher prevalence in developing regions. The carcinogenic pathway is a well-mapped sequence known as the Correa cascade: chronic active gastritis → atrophic gastritis → intestinal metaplasia → dysplasia → adenocarcinoma. Decades of inflammation generate reactive oxygen species and DNA damage, and strains carrying the cagA pathogenicity island inject the CagA protein directly into epithelial cells, disrupting cell polarity and signaling. Infected individuals carry roughly a 2–6 fold increased risk of gastric adenocarcinoma, and H. pylori is estimated to account for the large majority of non-cardia gastric cancers worldwide. The WHO/IARC classified it as a Group 1 carcinogen in 1994 — the first bacterium ever so designated. H. pylori is also the cause of most peptic ulcers and the only known infectious cause of a cancer that can be cured with antibiotics: gastric MALT lymphoma frequently regresses completely with eradication therapy alone. The 2005 Nobel Prize went to Barry Marshall and Robin Warren for establishing the link, famously after Marshall drank a culture of the organism and gave himself gastritis. Other real risk factors — high-salt and nitrate-preserved diets, smoking, Epstein–Barr virus, pernicious anemia, and hereditary CDH1 mutations — are genuine but much weaker or much rarer. The question asks for the strongest in the world, which is H. pylori both by effect size and by sheer number of people exposed.
questions.explanation:
The answer is infection of the stomach with Helicobacter pylori (H. pylori). H. pylori is a spiral-shaped bacterium that can live in the stomach's mucus layer, even though the stomach is very acidic. Many people around the world carry it.

Over many years, the infection causes long-term inflammation of the stomach lining (gastritis). This damage can slowly change the stomach cells, raising the risk of stomach cancer. H. pylori is also the main cause of stomach and duodenal ulcers. Treating it with antibiotics lowers these risks.

Big idea: some cancers and ulcers of the digestive system are caused by infections. Knowing the cause helps doctors prevent and treat them.

questions.prompt: Before the introduction of highly potent acid suppressive medications (proton pump inhibitors), a surgical procedure involving the cutting of a nerve was more commonly performed to treat peptic ulcer disease. What is the name of this procedure?
questions.answer: Vagotomy (cutting the vagus nerve, cranial nerve X)
questions.advancedExplanation: Vagotomy is surgical division of the vagus nerve — cranial nerve X — or of its gastric branches. Its logic follows directly from #34: the vagus provides the cephalic phase of gastric secretion, releasing acetylcholine that acts on parietal cell M3 receptors directly, stimulates ECL cells to release histamine, and stimulates G cells to release gastrin. Cutting it removes the largest single stimulatory input to acid production. Before H2 blockers (1970s) and proton pump inhibitors (late 1980s), and before the role of H. pylori was accepted, this was a mainstay of ulcer surgery. Three variants were performed, in increasing order of selectivity. Truncal vagotomy divides the anterior and posterior vagal trunks at the esophageal hiatus; it is simple and effective but denervates the pylorus and the rest of the abdominal viscera, so gastric emptying fails and a drainage procedure — pyloroplasty or gastrojejunostomy — must be added. Selective vagotomy spares the hepatic and celiac branches. Highly selective (parietal cell or proximal gastric) vagotomy divides only the nerves of Latarjet supplying the acid-producing fundus and body while preserving the antral and pyloric innervation, so no drainage procedure is needed — the most refined version, with the lowest side-effect rate but a higher ulcer recurrence rate. The procedure is now rare, performed mainly for complications such as perforation or bleeding, because ulcer disease turned out to be largely an infectious disease treatable with a two-week course of antibiotics plus a PPI. Its characteristic complications — dumping syndrome, diarrhea, delayed emptying — are a good illustration of what happens when you treat a signaling problem by cutting the cable.
questions.explanation:
The answer is a vagotomy, which means cutting the vagus nerve (cranial nerve X). The vagus nerve carries signals from the brain to the stomach. One of its jobs is to release acetylcholine, which tells the stomach to make acid.

Ulcers (sores in the stomach or duodenum) get worse with too much acid. Cutting the vagus nerve reduced acid production and helped ulcers heal. Today, medicines called proton pump inhibitors block acid so well that this surgery is rarely needed, and antibiotics can cure the H. pylori infection that causes many ulcers.

Big idea: the nervous system helps control digestion. Treatments for digestive diseases can target nerves, hormones, or the cells that make acid.

questions.prompt: Consumption of fatty foods or beverages before ingesting alcoholic beverages decreases the rate of alcohol intoxication. Explain the mechanism by which this occurs in relation to where and how alcohol is absorbed from the GI tract.
questions.answer: Consumption of fats delays gastric emptying by increasing secretion of GI hormones such as cholecystokinin and secretin (1 point). Alcohol can be absorbed directly through the stomach lining, but it is absorbed much more rapidly in the small intestine because of its vastly greater surface area (1 point). Delayed gastric emptying from fat consumption therefore slows alcohol absorption by keeping the alcohol in the stomach longer (1 point).
questions.advancedExplanation: Point 1 — fat delays gastric emptying. Lipid arriving in the duodenum triggers I cells to release cholecystokinin and K cells to release GIP, and activates the enterogastric reflex. CCK contracts the pyloric sphincter and inhibits gastric motility. The teleology is sound: fat is the slowest macronutrient to digest, so the duodenum signals the stomach to meter it out slowly. A fatty meal can extend gastric emptying from roughly 1–2 hours to 4 hours or more. Point 2 — where alcohol is absorbed. Ethanol is a small, uncharged, amphipathic molecule that crosses membranes by simple diffusion and needs no transporter or digestion. It therefore begins absorbing immediately through the gastric mucosa. But the stomach's absorptive surface is small and flat, while the small intestine — with plicae circulares, villi, and microvilli — presents on the order of 200 m². Roughly 80% or more of ingested alcohol is absorbed in the duodenum and jejunum, and absorption there is far faster per unit time than in the stomach. Point 3 — the two points combine. Since the rate-limiting step is delivery to the small intestine, anything that keeps alcohol in the stomach flattens the blood alcohol curve. Fat-induced delay in gastric emptying means alcohol trickles into the duodenum instead of arriving as a bolus, so peak blood alcohol concentration is lower and later even though the total amount eventually absorbed is similar. Conversely, drinking on an empty stomach — especially a carbonated drink, which accelerates emptying — produces a rapid spike. A secondary mechanism worth mentioning for a complete answer: time spent in the stomach also increases first-pass metabolism by gastric alcohol dehydrogenase in the mucosa, and whatever is absorbed from the stomach drains into the portal vein and passes through the liver before reaching the systemic circulation. Both effects reduce how much ethanol reaches the brain. (Gastric ADH activity is lower in women and is inhibited by some H2 blockers, which partly explains sex differences in blood alcohol after identical doses.) Key text note. The official key reads "increasing secretion of GI hormones such as cholecystokinin and secretion." This is a typographical error for secretin. Both CCK and secretin are released by the duodenum in response to chyme and both inhibit gastric emptying; the intended list is "cholecystokinin and secretin."
questions.explanation:
Eating fatty food first slows down how fast the stomach empties. When fat reaches the small intestine, the intestine releases hormones (like cholecystokinin and secretin) that tell the stomach to hold its contents longer.

Alcohol can be absorbed a little through the stomach wall, but it is absorbed much faster in the small intestine, because the small intestine has a huge surface area (folds, villi, and microvilli). If the stomach empties slowly, the alcohol stays in the stomach longer and reaches the small intestine more slowly, so it gets into the blood more slowly.

Big idea: the stomach acts like a holding tank, and hormones from the small intestine control how fast it empties. Most absorption happens in the small intestine because of its large surface area.

questions.prompt: Where are Brunner’s glands located in the GI tract? What are their function?
questions.answer: Duodenum (1 point); they secrete a bicarbonate-rich (alkaline) mucus that neutralizes stomach acid and protects the duodenal epithelium (1 point).
questions.advancedExplanation: Location (1 point). Brunner's glands (duodenal glands) are branched tubuloacinar glands found in the submucosa of the duodenum, concentrated in the first part (the duodenal bulb) and thinning out distally; they are essentially gone by the jejunum. Their location is histologically diagnostic — they are the only glands in the entire alimentary canal that sit in the submucosa, and their presence is how you identify duodenum under the microscope at a glance. Their ducts pierce the muscularis mucosae to empty into the intestinal crypts (crypts of Lieberkühn). Function (1 point). They secrete a thick, alkaline, bicarbonate-rich mucus. Chyme leaving the stomach has a pH of roughly 2, and the duodenal epithelium — unlike the gastric epithelium — has no thick protective mucus-bicarbonate barrier of its own. Brunner's gland secretion neutralizes the incoming acid and coats the mucosa, protecting it from peptic injury and simultaneously raising luminal pH toward the 6–8 range at which pancreatic enzymes, particularly trypsin and lipase, actually function. Their secretion is stimulated by secretin and vagal input and inhibited by sympathetic stimulation — which is one proposed reason chronic stress is associated with duodenal ulcers. The clinical correlate ties the anatomy together: duodenal ulcers occur overwhelmingly in the first part of the duodenum, precisely where acid load is highest, and Brunner's gland hyperplasia is a common response to chronic acid exposure. Do not confuse these with the crypts of Lieberkühn, which are mucosal glands present along the whole small and large intestine and which secrete intestinal juice and house Paneth and stem cells, or with goblet cells, which are single mucus-secreting cells within the epithelium.
questions.explanation:
Brunner's glands are found in the duodenum, the first part of the small intestine, in the layer under the lining (the submucosa). They make an alkaline (basic) mucus that is rich in bicarbonate.

Food leaving the stomach is very acidic. Brunner's glands' mucus neutralizes that acid and coats the lining of the duodenum, protecting it from being damaged. This helps prevent duodenal ulcers and gives intestinal enzymes the less acidic conditions they need to work.

Big idea: each part of the digestive tract protects itself from the materials passing through. The duodenum needs extra protection because it receives acid straight from the stomach.

questions.prompt: Write the correct name of the structure labeled 91 in the diagram.
questions.advancedExplanation: The innermost tunic, bracketed from the luminal surface down to and including the muscularis mucosae. It has three sublayers: the epithelium (simple columnar with absorptive enterocytes, goblet cells, and enteroendocrine cells), the lamina propria (loose connective tissue with capillaries, lacteals, and immune cells), and the muscularis mucosae (#100). This is the layer that does the absorbing and the layer that is biopsied endoscopically.
questions.explanation:
Label 91 is the mucosa, the innermost layer of the intestinal wall. It includes the villi and glands that face the inside of the intestine.

The mucosa absorbs nutrients and releases mucus and enzymes. It is made of an epithelium (lining cells), a thin layer of connective tissue, and a thin layer of muscle.

Big idea: the alimentary canal has four layers. From the inside out: mucosa, submucosa, muscularis externa, and serosa.

questions.prompt: Write the correct name of the structure labeled 92 in the diagram.
questions.advancedExplanation: The dense irregular connective tissue layer beneath the mucosa, bracketed at the band containing the large vessels. It is the structural and supply layer: it carries the larger arteries, veins, and lymphatics (#99, #101) and houses the submucosal plexus (#102). In the duodenum it uniquely contains Brunner's glands (#45) — the only glands in the submucosa anywhere in the gut. Because it carries the blood supply and the collagen, the submucosa is the layer that holds surgical sutures.
questions.explanation:
Label 92 is the submucosa, the layer just outside the mucosa.

The submucosa is connective tissue that holds the larger blood vessels, lymph vessels, and a network of nerves (the submucosal plexus).

Big idea: the submucosa supports the mucosa and supplies it with blood and nerves.

questions.prompt: Write the correct name of the structure labeled 93 in the diagram.
questions.advancedExplanation: The bracket spanning both muscle layers — the inner circular (#103) and the outer longitudinal (#105) — together with the myenteric plexus between them (#104). Also called the muscularis propria. This is the motility layer: circular contraction narrows the lumen and longitudinal contraction shortens the segment, and coordinated sequential firing produces peristalsis, while out-of-phase local contractions produce segmentation for mixing.
questions.explanation:
Label 93 is the muscularis externa (also called the muscularis propria), the thick muscle layer.

It has two layers of smooth muscle, circular and longitudinal. They squeeze in waves (peristalsis) to push food along and mix it (segmentation).

Big idea: the muscularis externa is the layer that moves food through the digestive tract.

questions.prompt: Write the correct name of the structure labeled 94 in the diagram.
questions.advancedExplanation: The thin outermost tunic: a layer of connective tissue covered by simple squamous mesothelium, continuous with the visceral peritoneum. Its mesothelial cells secrete serous fluid that lets intestinal loops slide against one another frictionlessly. The key allows "adventitia," which is the correct term where the tunic is a retroperitoneal binding layer instead — the esophagus, the duodenum's second and third parts, the ascending and descending colon, and the rectum. The intraperitoneal small intestine shown here properly has serosa.
questions.explanation:
Label 94 is the serosa, the outermost layer of the intestinal wall.

The serosa is a thin, slippery covering (part of the visceral peritoneum) that lets the intestines slide against each other without friction. In places like the esophagus, the outer layer is a tougher covering called adventitia instead.

Big idea: the four layers of the gut wall, from inside to outside, are mucosa, submucosa, muscularis externa, and serosa.

questions.prompt: Write the correct name of the structure labeled 95 in the diagram.
questions.advancedExplanation: The finger-like projections of mucosa into the lumen, 0.5–1.5 mm tall, each with a connective-tissue core containing a capillary network and a central lacteal. They are the second of the three tiers of surface amplification (plicae circulares → villi → microvilli), together multiplying absorptive area roughly 600-fold. Note the distinction from plicae circulares of #39: plicae are large permanent folds of mucosa and submucosa; villi are much smaller and are mucosa only. Villous atrophy — their flattening — is the histologic hallmark of celiac disease.
questions.explanation:
Label 95 is the villi (one is a villus). They are the finger-like projections sticking into the inside of the intestine.

Villi greatly increase the surface area for absorbing nutrients. Each villus has blood capillaries and a lacteal inside it to carry nutrients away.

Big idea: the small intestine uses folds, villi, and microvilli to create a huge absorbing surface.

questions.prompt: Write the correct name of the structure labeled 96 in the diagram.
questions.advancedExplanation: The tubular invagination of epithelium descending between the bases of the villi — the inverse of a villus. Crypts house the intestinal stem cells that continuously regenerate the entire epithelium every 3–5 days, Paneth cells at the base secreting defensins and lysozyme to protect those stem cells, and cells secreting intestinal juice. The crypt–villus axis is a conveyor: cells are born in the crypt, migrate up the villus maturing as they go, and are shed at the tip.
questions.explanation:
Label 96 is an intestinal gland, also called an intestinal crypt (crypt of Lieberkuhn). It is the pocket that dips down between the villi.

The crypts hold stem cells that constantly make new lining cells, plus cells that release mucus and germ-fighting proteins.

Big idea: the intestinal lining is replaced every few days, and the new cells come from the crypts.

questions.prompt: Write the correct name of the structure labeled 97 in the diagram.
questions.advancedExplanation: The round, densely stippled structure within the lamina propria, its speckled appearance representing packed lymphocytes. A solitary lymphoid follicle is a B-cell aggregate, often with a germinal center, belonging to the gut-associated lymphoid tissue. In the ileum these follicles cluster into the Peyer's patches of #90 — the two labels describe the same tissue at different scales, which is the connection this figure is drawing.
questions.explanation:
Label 97 is a lymphoid follicle (lymphoid nodule), the round, dotted mass in the mucosa.

It is a cluster of lymphocytes that watches for germs. Groups of these follicles in the ileum form Peyer's patches.

Big idea: the digestive tract has its own immune tissue because food can carry germs.

questions.prompt: Write the correct name of the structure labeled 98 in the diagram.
questions.advancedExplanation: The green blind-ended vessel running up the center of a villus. It is a lymphatic capillary, distinguishable from the villus's blood capillaries by its central position, blind ending, and larger caliber. Its endothelium has loose overlapping junctions and discontinuous basement membrane, making it permeable to chylomicrons too large to enter blood capillaries — which is the structural reason dietary fat takes the lymphatic route (see #65).
