The name comes from lac, milk.
questions.explanation:
Label 98 is a lacteal, the lymph vessel running up the middle of a villus.

Lacteals absorb digested fats, which are packed into chylomicrons that are too big to enter blood capillaries. The fatty lymph (chyle) is carried through the lymphatic system into the blood.

Big idea: most nutrients enter the blood capillaries in the villi, but fats enter the lacteals.

questions.prompt: Write the correct name of the structure labeled 99 in the diagram.
questions.advancedExplanation: Two leaders point to the paired red and blue vessels in the submucosa. These are the supplying and draining vessels from which the villous capillary networks arise; the venous side drains to the portal vein, carrying absorbed sugars and amino acids to the liver for first-pass metabolism — the contrast that makes the lacteal's bypass in #98 significant.
questions.explanation:
Label 99 is the submucosal arteriole and venule (submucosal blood vessels), the red and blue vessels in the submucosa.

These vessels bring blood to the intestinal wall and carry away absorbed nutrients. The blue venules drain toward the hepatic portal vein, which takes nutrient-rich blood to the liver.

Big idea: the submucosa is the layer that carries the main blood supply of the gut wall.

questions.prompt: Write the correct name of the structure labeled 100 in the diagram.
questions.advancedExplanation: The thin band of smooth muscle forming the deepest layer of the mucosa, separating mucosa from submucosa. Do not confuse it with the muscularis externa (#93): this is a thin sheet whose contraction agitates the villi and folds the mucosa to improve contact with chyme, not a propulsive layer. It is also the critical staging boundary in GI oncology — a carcinoma that has not breached it is intramucosal, with essentially no metastatic potential, because the mucosa above it has no lymphatics.
questions.explanation:
Label 100 is the muscularis mucosa (muscularis mucosae), a thin layer of smooth muscle at the bottom of the mucosa.

This thin muscle layer makes the mucosa wiggle and fold, helping it contact food. Do not confuse it with the much thicker muscularis externa farther out.

Big idea: the mucosa has its own thin muscle layer, separate from the main muscle layer of the gut wall.

questions.prompt: Write the correct name of the structure labeled 101 in the diagram.
questions.advancedExplanation: The green vessel within the submucosa, distinguished from the red and blue blood vessels of #99 by color. This is the collecting lymphatic into which the villous lacteals (#98) drain; from here chyle passes to the mesenteric lymphatics, the cisterna chyli (#89), and the thoracic duct (#85).
questions.explanation:
Label 101 is a lymphatic duct (lymph vessel), the green vessel in the submucosa.

It carries lymph, including fat from the lacteals, out of the intestinal wall toward larger lymph vessels.

Big idea: lymph vessels drain the gut wall and carry absorbed fat and immune cells.

questions.prompt: Write the correct name of the structure labeled 102 in the diagram.
questions.advancedExplanation: The yellow nerve network within the submucosa. With the myenteric plexus it forms the enteric nervous system — some 500 million neurons, enough to operate autonomously, which is why the gut is called the "second brain." Meissner's plexus sits close to the epithelium and primarily controls secretion, local blood flow, and mucosal/muscularis mucosae movement. Position is the discriminator: submucosa → Meissner's; between the muscle layers → Auerbach's.
questions.explanation:
Label 102 is the submucosal plexus (Meissner's plexus), a network of nerves in the submucosa.

This nerve network controls the glands and blood flow of the mucosa. It is part of the enteric nervous system, the gut's own 'little brain'.

Big idea: the gut has its own nervous system that can control digestion even without the brain.

questions.prompt: Write the correct name of the structure labeled 103 in the diagram.
questions.advancedExplanation: The inner of the two muscularis externa layers, nearer the lumen. Its fibers encircle the gut, so contraction narrows the lumen and, propagating distally behind a bolus, produces peristalsis. Its local thickenings form the sphincters. The orientation is read from the cut faces: on the face where these fibers run as long strands, the layer is cut parallel to its fibers; on the perpendicular face the same layer appears as polygonal cross-sections.
questions.explanation:
Label 103 is the circular layer of the muscularis externa, the inner muscle layer.

Its fibers wrap around the tube. When they contract, the tube gets narrower, squeezing food along. Thickened circular muscle forms sphincters, like the pyloric sphincter.

Big idea: circular and longitudinal muscle work together to produce peristalsis.

questions.prompt: Write the correct name of the structure labeled 104 in the diagram.
questions.advancedExplanation: The yellow nerve network sandwiched between the circular and longitudinal muscle layers — the position its name describes (myo-enteric). It controls gut motility: the frequency and force of contraction and the coordination of peristalsis. Its congenital absence in a segment of distal colon, from failed neural crest migration, is Hirschsprung disease, in which the aganglionic segment cannot relax and the bowel proximal to it dilates massively. Loss of myenteric inhibitory neurons in the lower esophagus causes achalasia.
questions.explanation:
Label 104 is the myenteric plexus (Auerbach's plexus), the nerve network between the two muscle layers.

It controls the muscles of the gut wall, setting how strong and how often they contract. It coordinates peristalsis.

Big idea: two nerve networks run the gut: the submucosal plexus (glands and blood flow) and the myenteric plexus (muscle movement).

questions.prompt: Write the correct name of the structure labeled 105 in the diagram.
questions.advancedExplanation: The outer muscle layer, with fibers running along the gut's long axis, so contraction shortens the segment and helps draw it over the bolus. In the colon this layer is not continuous but gathered into the three taeniae coli, whose shortness puckers the wall into the haustra of #39. Its appearance on the two cut faces is the mirror image of #103 — polygonal where the circular layer is fibrous, and fibrous where the circular layer is polygonal.
questions.explanation:
Label 105 is the longitudinal layer of the muscularis externa, the outer muscle layer.

Its fibers run along the length of the tube. When they contract, the tube gets shorter. Together with the circular layer, it pushes food forward.

Big idea: the gut wall has an inner circular and an outer longitudinal layer of smooth muscle.

questions.prompt: Which of the following organs is shared by the digestive and respiratory systems?

choices.explanation: Incorrect. The diaphragm is a breathing muscle, not a passage for food.
Incorrect. The esophagus carries only food to the stomach.
Incorrect. The intercostal muscles help with breathing only.
Incorrect. The larynx carries only air; food should never enter it.
Correct. The pharynx carries both air and food.
Incorrect. The trachea carries only air.

questions.explanation:
The answer is the pharynx (throat). Both air and food pass through the pharynx. Air goes from the nose through the pharynx into the larynx; food goes from the mouth through the pharynx into the esophagus.

The esophagus is only for food, and the larynx and trachea are only for air. The diaphragm and intercostal muscles help with breathing but are not passageways for food.

Big idea: the pharynx is a shared hallway for the respiratory and digestive systems, which is why the body needs the epiglottis to keep food out of the airway.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is not part of the gastrointestinal tract?

choices.explanation: Incorrect. The cecum is the first part of the large intestine.
Incorrect. The esophagus carries food to the stomach.
Incorrect. The stomach is a main part of the GI tract.
Incorrect. The mouth is where the GI tract begins.
Incorrect. The pharynx carries food from the mouth to the esophagus.
Correct. The spleen is an immune organ; food never passes through it.

questions.explanation:
The answer is the spleen. The gastrointestinal (GI) tract, also called the alimentary canal, is the long tube food travels through: mouth, pharynx, esophagus, stomach, small intestine, large intestine (including the cecum), rectum, and anus.

The spleen sits near the stomach, but food never passes through it. It is an organ of the immune and blood systems that filters blood.

Big idea: the GI tract is the tube food moves through. Other organs nearby, like the liver and pancreas, help digestion from the outside, and some, like the spleen, are not digestive at all.

questions.prompt: In a healthy human, the digestion of proteins is most likely to begin in the:

choices.explanation: Incorrect. The cecum is in the large intestine, after most digestion is done.
Incorrect. The duodenum continues protein digestion, but it starts in the stomach.
Incorrect. The ileum is mostly for absorption.
Incorrect. The jejunum continues digestion and absorption but is not where protein digestion begins.
Incorrect. Saliva has no protein-digesting enzymes.
Correct. Pepsin and stomach acid begin protein digestion in the stomach.

questions.explanation:
The answer is the stomach. Protein digestion starts in the stomach, where cells release hydrochloric acid and an enzyme called pepsin.

The acid unfolds proteins and turns inactive pepsinogen into active pepsin, which starts cutting proteins into smaller pieces. Digestion of proteins finishes in the small intestine with enzymes from the pancreas and the intestinal lining. The mouth starts carbohydrate digestion, not protein digestion.

Big idea: different nutrients start being digested in different places: carbohydrates in the mouth, proteins in the stomach, and fats mostly in the small intestine.

questions.prompt: The salivary gland that secretes into the month from under the tongue is:

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Lingual glands are tiny glands in the tongue, not one of the major salivary glands.
Incorrect. The parotid duct opens on the inside of the cheek, not under the tongue.
Incorrect. 'Pharyngeal' is not a salivary gland.
Incorrect for this key. The sublingual glands also drain under the tongue, but the key is the submandibular gland, whose large duct opens under the tongue.
Correct. The submandibular gland's duct opens on the floor of the mouth under the tongue.
Incorrect. The uvula hangs from the soft palate and is not a gland.

questions.explanation:
The official answer is the submandibular gland. There are three pairs of large salivary glands: the parotid glands (in front of the ears), the submandibular glands (under the jaw), and the sublingual glands (under the tongue).

The submandibular gland sits under the jaw, but its duct runs forward and opens on the floor of the mouth, right under the tongue next to the tongue's 'string' (frenulum). The sublingual glands also lie under the tongue and drain there through many small ducts. The parotid duct opens on the inside of the cheek near the upper molars.

Big idea: salivary glands make saliva, which starts carbohydrate digestion and makes food easy to swallow.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is not a function of saliva?

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Saliva does dilute food, so this is a real function.
Correct. Saliva never touches the arteries, so this is not one of its functions.

choices.text: Secretion of enzymes that digest starches and lipids
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Saliva contains amylase for starch, and glands on the tongue add lipase for fats, so this is a real function.

choices.text: Secretion of hydrochloric acid to initiate acidification
choices.explanation: Correct. Hydrochloric acid is made in the stomach, not by salivary glands.

choices.text: Secretion of mucus to prevent damage to the esophagus
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Mucus in saliva lubricates food so it does not scrape the esophagus, so this is a real function.

choices.text: Traps bacteria to prevent it from entering the lungs
choices.explanation: Correct. Keeping germs out of the lungs is the job of airway mucus and cilia, not saliva.

questions.explanation:
The answers are 'moisten and smooth the arteries', 'secretion of hydrochloric acid', and 'traps bacteria to prevent it from entering the lungs'. These are things saliva does NOT do.

Saliva stays in the digestive tract, so it never touches arteries. Hydrochloric acid is made by the stomach, not the salivary glands. Trapping germs before they reach the lungs is the job of mucus and cilia in the airways. Saliva does dilute food, contain enzymes (amylase for starch and, from tongue glands, a little lipase for fats), and contain mucus that helps food slide down the esophagus.

Big idea: saliva moistens food, starts chemical digestion, and protects the mouth. It is part of the digestive system, not the respiratory or circulatory systems.

questions.prompt: Which layer of the digestive tract is most responsible for peristalsis?

choices.explanation: Incorrect. The lumen is the hollow space inside the tube, not a layer of the wall.
Incorrect. The mesentery is a sheet that holds the intestines in place; it does not squeeze.
Incorrect. The mucosa is the inner lining that absorbs and secretes.
Correct. The muscularis contracts in waves to cause peristalsis.
Incorrect. The serosa is the thin outer covering.
Incorrect. The submucosa holds blood vessels and nerves, not the main muscles.

questions.explanation:
The answer is the muscularis (muscularis externa). Peristalsis is a wave of muscle squeezing that pushes food along the digestive tract, like squeezing toothpaste from a tube.

The muscularis is the thick muscle layer of the gut wall. It has an inner circular layer and an outer longitudinal layer of smooth muscle that work together to make these waves. The mucosa lines the inside, the submucosa holds blood vessels and nerves, and the serosa is the slippery outer covering. The lumen is the empty space inside the tube.

Big idea: the gut wall has four layers, and each has a job. Movement comes from the muscularis.

questions.prompt: Most of food digestion takes place in the:

choices.explanation: Incorrect. The large intestine absorbs water and salts; little digestion happens there.
Incorrect. The liver makes bile, but food does not pass through it.
Incorrect. The pancreas makes enzymes, but they work in the small intestine.
Incorrect. Salivary glands start starch digestion only.
Correct. Most digestion happens in the small intestine.
Incorrect. The stomach starts protein digestion, but most digestion happens later.

questions.explanation:
The answer is the small intestine. Most chemical digestion and nearly all absorption of nutrients happen in the small intestine.

Enzymes from the pancreas and from the intestinal lining, plus bile from the liver, finish breaking down carbohydrates, proteins, and fats there. The stomach only starts protein digestion. The liver and pancreas make digestive juices, but food never goes through them. The large intestine mainly absorbs water.

Big idea: the small intestine is the main place where food is digested and absorbed.

questions.prompt: What is the first type of macromolecule to be worked on by enzymes after ingestion?

choices.explanation: Correct. Salivary amylase starts carbohydrate (starch) digestion in the mouth.
Incorrect. Most fat digestion happens in the small intestine.
Incorrect. Nucleic acids are digested in the small intestine by pancreatic enzymes.
Incorrect. Peptides are broken down later in the stomach and small intestine.
Incorrect. Protein digestion begins in the stomach, after carbohydrates.
Incorrect. Simple sugars do not need much digestion; the enzyme in the mouth works on starch.

questions.explanation:
The answer is carbohydrates. As soon as food enters the mouth, the enzyme salivary amylase starts breaking starch (a carbohydrate) into smaller sugars.

Proteins are not worked on until they reach the stomach (pepsin), and most fat digestion happens in the small intestine. 'Sugars' is a kind of carbohydrate, but the starch-digesting enzyme acts on large carbohydrates like starch.

Big idea: digestion of each type of macromolecule begins in a different place, and carbohydrates come first.

questions.prompt: The region of the stomach that acts as temporary storage for ingested food is the:

choices.explanation: Incorrect. The antrum grinds and mixes food, near the exit.
Incorrect for this key. The body holds and mixes food too, but the fundus is the expected storage region.
Incorrect. The cardia is just where the esophagus enters.
Correct. The fundus is the dome-shaped top part that stores food.
Incorrect. The pyloric canal leads to the exit of the stomach.
Incorrect. The pylorus controls the exit of food into the duodenum.

questions.explanation:
The answer is the fundus. The stomach has several regions: the cardia (where the esophagus enters), the fundus (the rounded top part), the body (the large middle), and the pyloric region (antrum, pyloric canal, and pylorus) leading to the small intestine.

The fundus bulges up above where the esophagus joins. Food and gas collect there, and the stomach can relax to store food before it is mixed and moved along. The body also stores food in many textbooks, but the fundus is the classic answer for storage. The pyloric region grinds and pushes food out.

Big idea: different parts of the stomach have different jobs: storing food, mixing it with acid, and passing it to the small intestine.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is true about the walls of the small and large intestines?

choices.text: The inner wall of the large intestine consists of villi to increase absorption
choices.explanation: Incorrect. The large intestine does not have villi.

choices.text: The inner wall of the small intestine consists of villi to increase absorption
choices.explanation: Correct. Villi in the small intestine increase the surface area for absorption.

choices.text: The outer layer of the large intestine wall is adventitia
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Most of the large intestine is covered by serosa, not adventitia.

choices.text: The outer layer of the small intestine wall is adventitia
choices.explanation: Incorrect. The small intestine's outer layer is serosa.

choices.text: The walls of the large intestine help in the absorption of electrolytes and salts
choices.explanation: Correct. The large intestine absorbs water, electrolytes, and salts.

choices.text: The walls of the small intestine help in the absorption of electrolytes and salts
choices.explanation: Incorrect for this key. The small intestine does absorb some salts, but the key credits the large intestine for this job.

questions.explanation:
The answers are that the small intestine has villi to increase absorption, and the large intestine absorbs electrolytes and salts. Villi are finger-like bumps in the small intestine's lining that greatly increase its surface area for absorbing nutrients. The large intestine has no villi.

The large intestine absorbs water, salts, and electrolytes (like sodium) to turn liquid waste into solid stool. The small intestine absorbs some salts too, but this key focuses on the large intestine's role. Both intestines are mostly covered on the outside by serosa, not adventitia.

Big idea: the small intestine is built to absorb nutrients (villi), and the large intestine is built to absorb water and salts.

questions.prompt: Undigested food residues move through the small intestine in the following sequence:

choices.explanation: Incorrect. The jejunum comes before the ileum.
Correct. Food moves through the duodenum, then the jejunum, then the ileum.
Incorrect. The ileum is the last part, not the first.
Incorrect. This is the order backwards.
Incorrect. The duodenum comes first, right after the stomach.
Incorrect. The duodenum comes first, not last.

questions.explanation:
The answer is duodenum, jejunum, ileum. Food leaving the stomach first enters the duodenum, a short C-shaped section. Next comes the jejunum, then the ileum, which connects to the large intestine.

A memory trick: 'Dow Jones Industrial', for Duodenum, Jejunum, Ileum.

Big idea: the small intestine has three parts in a fixed order, and each has a slightly different job: mixing with digestive juices (duodenum), absorbing nutrients (jejunum), and absorbing vitamin B12 and bile salts (ileum).

questions.prompt: The main function of the jejunum is:

choices.explanation: Correct. The jejunum's main job is absorbing nutrients.
Incorrect. Water absorption is finished in the large intestine.
Incorrect. Most chemical digestion happens earlier, in the duodenum.
Incorrect. Waste is expelled through the rectum and anus.

choices.text: Increasing the pH of digested material after it leaves the stomach
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Neutralizing acid happens in the duodenum.
Incorrect. Mechanical digestion mainly happens in the mouth and stomach.

questions.explanation:
The answer is absorption of nutrients. The jejunum, the middle part of the small intestine, has tall villi and many folds, giving it a huge surface area. Most sugars, amino acids, and fats are absorbed here.

Water is absorbed mostly in the small intestine overall and finished in the large intestine. Expelling waste is the job of the rectum and anus. The duodenum is where stomach acid gets neutralized (pH increases) and most chemical digestion happens.

Big idea: the small intestine is where nutrients enter the body, and the jejunum is the main absorbing section.

questions.prompt: For those who have lactose intolerance caused by lactase deficiency, their bodies cannot break down lactose into which of these simpler forms?

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Amylose is a part of starch, not something lactose breaks into.
Incorrect. Amylopectin is a part of starch.
Incorrect. Cellulose is plant fiber, not part of lactose.
Correct. Galactose is one of the two sugars in lactose.
Correct. Glucose is the other sugar in lactose.
Incorrect. Sucrose is table sugar (glucose + fructose), a different disaccharide.

questions.explanation:
The answers are galactose and glucose. Lactose, the sugar in milk, is a disaccharide, which means it is made of two simple sugars stuck together: one glucose and one galactose.

The enzyme lactase splits lactose into glucose and galactose so they can be absorbed. Without enough lactase, lactose cannot be split. Sucrose (table sugar) is a different disaccharide (glucose + fructose). Amylose and amylopectin are the two parts of starch, and cellulose is plant fiber that humans cannot digest.

Big idea: each disaccharide is split by its own enzyme into two simple sugars. Lactase splits lactose.

questions.prompt: Eating:

choices.text: Exacerbates the pain in duodenal ulcers
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Eating usually eases duodenal ulcer pain at first.

choices.text: Exacerbates the pain in gastric ulcers
choices.explanation: Correct. Eating triggers acid that irritates a gastric ulcer.
Correct. Eating can increase discomfort from an inflamed liver.

choices.text: Reduces the pain in duodenal ulcers
choices.explanation: Correct. Food buffers the acid, so duodenal ulcer pain often eases after eating.

choices.text: Reduces the pain in gastric ulcers
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Eating usually makes gastric ulcer pain worse.
Incorrect. Eating does not relieve hepatitis pain.

questions.explanation:
The answers are that eating makes gastric ulcer pain worse, makes hepatitis pain worse, and reduces duodenal ulcer pain. An ulcer is an open sore in the lining of the stomach (gastric ulcer) or the first part of the small intestine (duodenal ulcer).

When you eat, the stomach makes acid, which irritates a gastric ulcer and makes it hurt more. A duodenal ulcer often feels better right after eating, because food buffers the acid and the stomach holds onto it for a while. Later, when acidic food moves into the duodenum, the pain comes back. In hepatitis, the liver is inflamed and swollen; eating, especially fatty food, makes the liver and gallbladder work harder and can increase the discomfort.

Big idea: when pain happens in relation to meals is a clue that helps doctors tell gastric ulcers from duodenal ulcers.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is not a site of mechanical digestion?

choices.explanation: Incorrect. The small intestine mixes food by segmentation, a form of mechanical digestion.
Incorrect. Chewing in the mouth is mechanical digestion.
Incorrect. The stomach churns food, which is mechanical digestion.
Correct. The large intestine mainly absorbs water; it is not a site of mechanical digestion.
Incorrect. One of the listed choices is right, so 'None of the above' does not apply.

questions.explanation:
The answer is the large intestine. Mechanical digestion means physically breaking food into smaller pieces or mixing it, without changing it chemically.

The mouth chews (mastication), the stomach churns and grinds food, and the small intestine mixes food with digestive juices by segmentation. By the time material reaches the large intestine, digestion is basically done; the large intestine mostly absorbs water and moves waste along, so it is not considered a site of mechanical digestion.

Big idea: mechanical digestion breaks food apart physically, which gives enzymes more surface to work on.

questions.prompt: Which of the following structures will never come in contact with ingested material?

choices.explanation: Incorrect. The jejunum is part of the small intestine, where food passes.
Incorrect. Food passes through the pyloric valve from the stomach to the duodenum.
Correct. The pancreatic acini make enzymes but never touch food.
Incorrect. The appendix opens into the large intestine, so material can enter it.
Incorrect. One of the listed choices is right, so 'None of the above' does not apply.

questions.explanation:
The answer is the acini. Acini are tiny clusters of cells in the pancreas (and salivary glands) that make digestive enzymes. The enzymes flow out through ducts into the small intestine, but food never travels back up into the acini.

The jejunum and the pyloric valve are part of the tube food passes through, and the appendix connects to the large intestine, so material can enter it.

Big idea: accessory organs like the pancreas help digestion from outside the tube; food never passes through them.

questions.prompt: Which organic molecules is digested by saliva?

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Nucleic acids are digested in the small intestine.
Incorrect. Fats are mainly digested in the small intestine.
Correct. Salivary amylase digests starch, a carbohydrate.
Incorrect. Protein digestion starts in the stomach.
Incorrect. One of the listed choices is right, so 'None of the above' does not apply.

questions.explanation:
The answer is carbohydrates. Saliva contains salivary amylase, an enzyme that breaks starch (a carbohydrate) into smaller sugars.

If you chew a cracker for a long time, it starts to taste sweet, because amylase is turning starch into sugar. Saliva has no real protein-digesting enzymes. (Glands on the tongue add a little lipase for fats, but saliva's main digestive job is starch.)

Big idea: chemical digestion of carbohydrates starts in the mouth.

questions.prompt: Which of the following stomach digestive cells secrete hydrochloric acid?

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Chief cells make pepsinogen, not acid.
Correct. Parietal cells make hydrochloric acid.
Incorrect. Enteroendocrine cells make hormones.
Incorrect. G cells make gastrin, a hormone that tells parietal cells to make acid.
Incorrect. One of the listed choices is right, so 'None of the above' does not apply.

questions.explanation:
The answer is parietal cells. Parietal cells in the stomach's gastric glands pump out hydrogen ions to make hydrochloric acid (HCl). They also make intrinsic factor, which is needed to absorb vitamin B12.

Chief cells make pepsinogen (which becomes the protein-digesting enzyme pepsin). G cells are enteroendocrine cells that make the hormone gastrin, which tells parietal cells to make more acid.

Big idea: different cells in the stomach lining each have a job: acid (parietal), enzymes (chief), and hormones (enteroendocrine, like G cells).

questions.prompt: Which structure separates the digestive tract and the respiratory tract when swallowing?

choices.explanation: Incorrect. The larynx is the airway opening that gets covered; the epiglottis does the covering.
Incorrect. The pleural cavity surrounds the lungs.
Incorrect. Alveoli are air sacs deep in the lungs.
Incorrect. The trachea is the airway that the epiglottis protects.
Correct. The right answer, the epiglottis, is not listed.

questions.explanation:
The answer is 'None of the above'. The structure that separates the digestive and respiratory tracts during swallowing is the epiglottis, and it is not listed.

The epiglottis is a flap of elastic cartilage at the top of the larynx. When you swallow, the larynx rises and the epiglottis tips down over its opening, so food slides into the esophagus instead of the trachea. The larynx is the opening being covered, not the cover. The pleural cavity, alveoli, and trachea are deeper parts of the respiratory system.

Big idea: the throat is shared by food and air, so the body needs a 'traffic controller', the epiglottis.

questions.prompt: Mastication occurs in the __________

choices.explanation: Correct. Chewing (mastication) happens in the mouth.
Incorrect. The esophagus moves food to the stomach by peristalsis.
Incorrect. The stomach churns food but does not chew it.
Incorrect. The colon absorbs water.
Incorrect. One of the listed choices is right, so 'None of the above' does not apply.

questions.explanation:
The answer is the mouth. Mastication means chewing. Teeth cut and grind food, the tongue moves it around, and saliva moistens it into a soft ball called a bolus.

Chewing is mechanical digestion: it breaks food into smaller pieces so enzymes can work on more surface area. The esophagus only moves food, the stomach churns (but does not chew), and the colon absorbs water.

Big idea: digestion starts in the mouth with both chewing (mechanical) and saliva (chemical).

questions.prompt: Which of the following enzyme is found in pancreatic juice?

choices.explanation: Correct. Nucleases digest DNA and RNA.
Correct. Pancreatic lipase digests fats.
Correct. Proteases like trypsin digest proteins.
Correct. Pancreatic amylase digests starch.
Incorrect. All of the listed enzymes are found in pancreatic juice.

questions.explanation:
The answers are nucleases, lipases, proteases, and amylases. Pancreatic juice is a mix of enzymes and bicarbonate that the pancreas sends into the duodenum.

It contains enzymes for every major type of nutrient: amylase for starch, lipase for fats, proteases (like trypsin and chymotrypsin) for proteins, and nucleases for DNA and RNA. The bicarbonate neutralizes stomach acid so these enzymes can work.

Big idea: the pancreas makes the most complete set of digestive enzymes in the body.

questions.prompt: Which of the following molecules are secreted by chief cells?

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Intrinsic factor is made by parietal cells.
Correct. Chief cells make pepsinogen.
Correct. Chief cells make gastric lipase.
Incorrect. Somatostatin is made by D cells, not chief cells.
Incorrect. Chief cells do not make intrinsic factor or somatostatin.

questions.explanation:
The answers are pepsinogen and lipases. Chief cells sit deep in the stomach's gastric glands. They release pepsinogen, an inactive enzyme that stomach acid turns into pepsin to digest proteins. They also release gastric lipase, which starts a little fat digestion.

Intrinsic factor is made by parietal cells, and somatostatin is a hormone made by D cells (a type of enteroendocrine cell). So 'All of the above' is not correct.

Big idea: each stomach cell type has its own product: chief cells make enzymes, parietal cells make acid and intrinsic factor, and enteroendocrine cells make hormones.

questions.prompt: Which part of the digestive system absorbs the most water?

choices.explanation: Incorrect for this key. The jejunum absorbs a lot of water along with nutrients, but the expected answer is the colon.
Correct. Absorbing water is the colon's main job.
Incorrect. The duodenum mostly mixes food with digestive juices.
Incorrect. The ileum absorbs vitamin B12 and bile salts.
Incorrect. One of the listed choices is right, so 'None of the above' does not apply.

questions.explanation:
The official answer is the colon. The colon's main job is to absorb water and salts from leftover material, turning liquid waste into solid stool.

Strictly speaking, the small intestine (especially the jejunum) absorbs a larger total amount of water, because it handles all the fluid you drink plus digestive juices. The colon absorbs the last remaining water. This question expects the colon, because absorbing water is the colon's main job.

Big idea: the small intestine absorbs nutrients and much of the water; the large intestine finishes water absorption and forms stool.

questions.prompt: In which part of the small intestine does the most chemical digestion occur?

choices.explanation: Incorrect. The ileum mostly absorbs nutrients, vitamin B12, and bile salts.
Correct. Pancreatic enzymes and bile enter the duodenum, so most chemical digestion happens there.
Incorrect. The jejunum mainly absorbs nutrients.
Incorrect. One of the listed choices is right, so 'None of the above' does not apply.

questions.explanation:
The answer is the duodenum. The duodenum is the first part of the small intestine. It receives partly digested food from the stomach, plus enzymes from the pancreas and bile from the liver and gallbladder.

Because all these digestive juices enter here, most chemical digestion happens in the duodenum. The jejunum and ileum mostly absorb the nutrients that have been broken down.

Big idea: the duodenum is the mixing station where digestive juices meet food.

questions.prompt: Brush border enzymes help to break down which of the following organic molecules?

choices.explanation: Correct. Brush border nucleosidases and phosphatases finish breaking down nucleic acids.
Incorrect. Fats are digested by pancreatic lipase, not brush border enzymes.
Correct. Brush border enzymes like lactase and sucrase split sugars.
Correct. Brush border peptidases finish protein digestion.
Incorrect. Brush border enzymes do help break down several of the listed molecules.

questions.note: The official key marks only C and D, but the brush border also has nucleosidases and phosphatases that break down nucleic acid pieces (A).
questions.explanation:
The answers are nucleic acids, carbohydrates, and proteins. The brush border is the fuzzy surface of microvilli on the cells lining the small intestine. Enzymes stuck to this surface finish digestion right where absorption happens.

Brush border enzymes include sugar-splitting enzymes (like lactase, sucrase, and maltase) for carbohydrates, peptidases for protein pieces, and nucleosidases and phosphatases for pieces of nucleic acids. Fats are digested by pancreatic lipase in the intestine's cavity, not by the brush border. (The official key only listed carbohydrates and proteins.)

Big idea: digestion finishes at the brush border, so nutrients are broken into the smallest units right before being absorbed.

questions.prompt: Intrinsic factor binds to vitamin ____ to make it absorbable

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Vitamin A is fat-soluble and is absorbed with fats.
Correct. Intrinsic factor binds vitamin B12 so it can be absorbed in the ileum.
Incorrect. Vitamin D is fat-soluble and absorbed with fats.
Incorrect. Vitamin E is fat-soluble and absorbed with fats.
Incorrect. Vitamin K is fat-soluble, and some is made by gut bacteria.

questions.explanation:
The answer is vitamin B12. Vitamin B12 cannot be absorbed by itself. Parietal cells in the stomach make a protein called intrinsic factor, which binds to B12.

The B12 and intrinsic factor travel together to the ileum (the last part of the small intestine), where special receptors absorb them. Without intrinsic factor, a person cannot absorb B12 and can develop anemia.

Big idea: some nutrients need special helpers to be absorbed. Vitamin B12 needs intrinsic factor.

questions.prompt: __________ is characterized by a sharp pain in the lower right abdomen

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Hepatitis affects the liver, in the upper right abdomen.
Incorrect. Colon cancer usually causes changes in bowel habits or bleeding, not classic sharp lower-right pain.
Incorrect. Salmonellosis (food poisoning) causes general cramps, diarrhea, and fever.
Incorrect. Diverticulosis usually causes no pain, or pain on the lower left when inflamed.
Correct. The answer, appendicitis, is not listed.

questions.explanation:
The answer is 'None of the above'. Sharp pain in the lower right abdomen is the classic sign of appendicitis, which is not listed.

The appendix is attached to the cecum in the lower right part of the abdomen. When it becomes blocked and inflamed, pain often starts around the belly button and moves to the lower right. Hepatitis causes pain in the upper right (where the liver is). Colon cancer and diverticulosis are usually not described this way, and salmonellosis causes general cramps and diarrhea.

Big idea: where pain is located helps doctors figure out which organ is affected.

questions.prompt: Which of the following hormones is not secreted by the small intestine?

choices.explanation: Incorrect. GIP is made by K cells in the small intestine.
Incorrect. Secretin is made by S cells in the small intestine.
Incorrect. Most of the body's serotonin is made by cells in the intestine.
Incorrect. D cells in the small intestine make somatostatin.
Correct. All four hormones are made in the small intestine.

questions.explanation:
The answer is 'None of the above', because all of the listed hormones are made in the small intestine. The small intestine contains many enteroendocrine cells that release hormones to control digestion.

GIP (glucose-dependent insulinotropic peptide) is made by K cells and helps release insulin after a meal. Secretin is made by S cells and tells the pancreas to release bicarbonate. Serotonin is made by enterochromaffin cells and helps control gut movement. Somatostatin is made by D cells and slows down many digestive processes.

Big idea: the gut is also a hormone-making organ that coordinates digestion.

questions.prompt: Which hepatitis type is spread through infected food?

choices.explanation: Correct. Hepatitis A spreads through contaminated food and water.
Incorrect. Hepatitis B spreads through blood and body fluids.
Incorrect. Hepatitis C spreads mainly through blood.
Incorrect. Hepatitis D spreads through blood and only infects people who have hepatitis B.
Incorrect. One of the listed choices is right, so 'None of the above' does not apply.

questions.explanation:
The answer is hepatitis A. Hepatitis A spreads by the fecal-oral route: tiny amounts of stool from an infected person get into food or water, often because of poor handwashing.

Hepatitis B, C, and D spread through blood and body fluids (for example, shared needles, sexual contact, or from mother to baby at birth). Hepatitis E also spreads through contaminated water. Hepatitis A usually causes a short illness that goes away, and a vaccine prevents it.

Big idea: different hepatitis viruses spread in different ways, so prevention is different too: handwashing and clean food for A, and avoiding blood exposure for B and C.

questions.prompt: Which of the following can cause or exacerbate peptic ulcers?

choices.explanation: Correct. H. pylori infection is the most common cause of peptic ulcers.
Correct. Caffeine increases stomach acid and can worsen ulcers.
Correct. NSAIDs weaken the stomach's protective lining.
Incorrect. Spicy foods do not cause ulcers.
Incorrect. Spicy foods do not cause ulcers, so not all choices are correct.

questions.explanation:
The answers are Helicobacter pylori, caffeine, and NSAIDs. A peptic ulcer is a sore in the lining of the stomach or duodenum.

The bacterium H. pylori is the most common cause, because it damages the protective mucus layer. NSAIDs (like ibuprofen and aspirin) are the second most common cause, because they reduce the chemicals that protect the stomach lining. Caffeine increases acid and can make ulcers worse. Spicy food does not cause ulcers (a common myth), although it may bother someone who already has one.

Big idea: ulcers happen when acid overwhelms the stomach's protection. H. pylori and NSAIDs are the main causes.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between peristalsis and segmentation.
questions.answer: Peristalsis is the contraction/relaxation of adjacent segments of the canals, moving the food along through propulsion. In segmentation, its the contraction/relaxation of nonadjacent segments, moving food forward then back, mix and mechanically breaking down food.
questions.explanation:
Both peristalsis and segmentation are muscle movements of the digestive tract, but they do different jobs.

Peristalsis is a wave of squeezing that moves along the tube in one direction, pushing food forward, like squeezing toothpaste out of a tube. Segmentation is when rings of muscle in separate spots squeeze and relax back and forth, chopping and mixing food with digestive juices without moving it much forward. Segmentation is common in the small intestine.

Big idea: peristalsis moves food along; segmentation mixes it.

questions.prompt: What is bile? Where is it secreted and what is its function?
questions.answer: Green-yellow alkaline fluid that contains many lipid molecules that help to emulsify large fat globules, separating them into smaller droplets, making them easier t digest.
questions.explanation:
Bile is a yellow-green, slightly basic (alkaline) liquid. It is made by the liver, stored and concentrated in the gallbladder, and released into the duodenum when fatty food arrives.

Bile does not contain digestive enzymes. Instead, its bile salts work like dish soap: they break big fat globules into tiny droplets. This is called emulsification. Smaller droplets have much more surface area, so the enzyme lipase can digest the fat much faster. Bile also carries waste, like bilirubin from old red blood cells, out of the body.

Big idea: bile helps fat digestion by emulsifying fat, not by chemically digesting it.

questions.prompt: Explain why some people are able to consume lactose and why some people are lactose intolerant. How does the bacteria within the colon relate to it?
questions.answer: Some people, usually by genetics, are unable to produce lactase, which breaks down lactose in the small intestine. It moves into the large intestine, where bacteria that can produce lactase break it down, but produce their own byproducts, like methane.
questions.explanation:
Lactose is the sugar in milk. To absorb it, the small intestine must split it into glucose and galactose using the enzyme lactase. People who make enough lactase can digest milk easily.

Many people make less lactase as they grow up; this depends a lot on their genes. Without enough lactase, lactose passes undigested into the colon. Bacteria in the colon eat the lactose and produce gases (like hydrogen, carbon dioxide, and methane) and acids. This causes bloating, gas, and cramps, and the undigested sugar pulls water into the gut, causing diarrhea.

Big idea: missing a digestive enzyme means food reaches the colon undigested, where bacteria ferment it.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference in function/presence between the rugae of the stomach and villi of the small intestine.
questions.answer: The rugae of the stomach are loose folds of the innermost layer, indicating that the stomach can extend to hold more than it appears. The villi, and microvilli, help to increase the overall surface area of the small intestine, to maximize nutrient absorption.
questions.explanation:
Rugae are large folds in the stomach's inner lining. When the stomach is empty, they are wrinkled up; when you eat a big meal, they flatten out so the stomach can stretch to hold more food.

Villi are tiny finger-like projections in the small intestine's lining, covered with even smaller microvilli. They greatly increase the surface area for absorbing nutrients. So rugae help with stretching (storage), while villi help with absorption.

Big idea: the shape of the lining matches each organ's job: stretchy storage in the stomach, huge absorbing surface in the small intestine.

questions.prompt: For the following organs, indicate whether mechanical digestion, chemical digestion, neither, or both occur there: mouth, esophagus, stomach, small intestine, large intestine. If there is chemical digestion, name one enzyme/substance that is used for chemical digestion.
questions.answer: Mouth- both (amylase, esophagus- neither, stomach- both (pepsin, gastric lipases), small intestine- both (any pancreatic enzymes), large intestine- both (bacteria fauna)
questions.explanation:
Mouth: both. Teeth chew food (mechanical), and salivary amylase starts digesting starch (chemical). Esophagus: neither. It just moves food to the stomach by peristalsis.

Stomach: both. It churns food (mechanical) and uses pepsin and acid (plus a little gastric lipase) for chemical digestion. Small intestine: both. Segmentation mixes food (mechanical), and pancreatic enzymes and brush border enzymes do most chemical digestion. Large intestine: mostly absorbs water; gut bacteria ferment leftover fiber, which is sometimes counted as chemical digestion.

Big idea: mechanical digestion breaks food apart physically, and chemical digestion uses enzymes and acids to change molecules.

questions.prompt: The structure labeled "1" in the diagram below is a(n)

choices.explanation: Correct. The finger-like projection of the intestinal lining is a villus.
Incorrect. A nephron is the filtering unit of the kidney.
Incorrect. A ureter carries urine from the kidney to the bladder.
Incorrect. The urethra carries urine out of the body.
Incorrect. The urinary meatus is the opening of the urethra.

questions.explanation:
The answer is a villus. The diagram shows the lining of the small intestine, with finger-like projections sticking up. The structure labeled 1 is one of those projections, called a villus (plural: villi).

Each villus contains tiny blood capillaries and a lymph vessel (lacteal) that absorb nutrients. The other choices (nephron, ureter, urethra, urinary meatus) are parts of the urinary system, which is not shown here.

Big idea: villi give the small intestine a huge surface area for absorbing digested food.

questions.prompt: Most of the products of digestion are absorbed into the circulatory system from the structure labeled with the number _____ on the diagram below.

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Label 1 is the liver, which makes bile but does not absorb food.
Incorrect. Label 2 is the gallbladder, which stores bile.
Incorrect. Label 3 is the large intestine, which mainly absorbs water.
Correct. Label 4 is the small intestine, where most nutrients are absorbed.
Incorrect. Label 5 is the stomach, which absorbs very little.

questions.explanation:
The answer is 4, which points to the small intestine. In the diagram, 1 is the liver, 2 is the gallbladder, 3 is the large intestine, 4 is the small intestine, and 5 is the stomach.

Most nutrients from digested food are absorbed into the blood through the walls of the small intestine, which has villi and microvilli to make a huge surface area. The stomach absorbs very little (some water and alcohol), and the large intestine mostly absorbs water.

Big idea: the small intestine is the main organ of absorption.

questions.prompt: Enzymes in saliva begin the chemical digestion of ____________.

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Most fat digestion happens in the small intestine.
Incorrect. Protein digestion starts in the stomach.
Correct. Salivary amylase starts breaking down starch.
Incorrect. Vitamins are absorbed, not digested by saliva.
Incorrect. Minerals are absorbed, not digested by enzymes.

questions.explanation:
The answer is carbohydrates. Saliva contains salivary amylase, an enzyme that starts breaking starch into smaller sugars.

Protein digestion starts in the stomach, and most fat digestion happens in the small intestine. Vitamins and minerals are absorbed, not digested by enzymes.

Big idea: carbohydrate digestion starts in the mouth.

questions.prompt: Pepsin and hydrochloric acid in the stomach begin the digestion of ______________.

choices.explanation: Correct. Pepsin and acid start protein digestion.
Incorrect. Starch digestion starts in the mouth with amylase.
Incorrect. Fat digestion mostly happens in the small intestine.
Incorrect. Carbohydrate digestion starts in the mouth.
Incorrect. Vitamins are absorbed without being digested.

questions.explanation:
The answer is proteins. In the stomach, hydrochloric acid unfolds proteins and activates pepsinogen into pepsin. Pepsin then cuts proteins into smaller pieces.

Starch and other carbohydrates start being digested in the mouth, and fats are mostly digested in the small intestine. Vitamins do not need digestion.

Big idea: the stomach is where protein digestion begins.

questions.prompt: The structure labeled "1" in the diagram below allows for an increase in _______________.

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Bile is made by the liver.
Incorrect. Acid is made in the stomach.
Incorrect. Villi do not grind food.
Correct. Villi increase surface area for absorbing nutrients.

questions.explanation:
The answer is nutrient absorption. Structure 1 in the diagram is a villus of the small intestine.

Thousands of villi stick out from the intestinal lining like the fibers of a towel, which hugely increases the surface area. More surface area means more nutrients can be absorbed into the blood and lymph. Villi do not make bile or acid, and they do not grind food.

Big idea: increasing surface area is a common way the body speeds up exchange, as in villi in the gut and alveoli in the lungs.

questions.prompt: The function of the digestive system is to

choices.explanation: Incorrect by itself. Chemical breakdown is one job, but not the only one.
Incorrect by itself. Mechanical breakdown is one job, but not the only one.
Incorrect by itself. Absorption is one job, but not the only one.
Correct. The digestive system does all three.

questions.explanation:
The answer is 'all of the above'. The digestive system breaks food apart mechanically (chewing, churning), breaks it down chemically (enzymes and acid), and absorbs the nutrients into the body.

It also gets rid of the leftover waste. Each step is needed: food must be broken into tiny molecules before it can be absorbed.

Big idea: the main jobs of the digestive system are ingestion, digestion (mechanical and chemical), absorption, and elimination.

questions.prompt: The wavelike contractions of muscle that move food through the digestive system are called _________________.

choices.explanation: Correct. Peristalsis is the wave-like muscle action that moves food along.
Incorrect. Most of the gut's movement is involuntary.
Incorrect. Mechanical digestion breaks food apart; it is not the name of these waves.
Incorrect. 'Involuntary digestion' is not the correct term.
Incorrect. Chemical digestion uses enzymes, not muscle waves.

questions.explanation:
The answer is peristalsis. Peristalsis is a wave of smooth muscle contraction that moves along the digestive tract, pushing food forward.

It happens automatically, even if you are upside down. Voluntary contractions only happen at the start (chewing, swallowing) and end (the anus). Mechanical and chemical digestion describe breaking food down, not moving it.

Big idea: peristalsis moves food through the digestive tube.

questions.prompt: Which statement(s) are correct about bile?

choices.text: Breaks down globules of fat into tiny droplets.
choices.explanation: Correct. Bile emulsifies fat into small droplets.
Incorrect. Bile is stored in the gallbladder.

choices.text: Is produced by the gall bladder
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Bile is produced by the liver.

choices.text: It is released into the large intestine.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Bile is released into the small intestine (duodenum).
Incorrect. Only statement A is true.

questions.explanation:
The answer is that bile breaks globules of fat into tiny droplets. This is called emulsification. It works like dish soap breaking up grease, giving the enzyme lipase more surface to work on.

The other statements are wrong: bile is produced by the liver (not the gallbladder), stored in the gallbladder (not the liver), and released into the small intestine (duodenum), not the large intestine. So 'all of the above' is also wrong.

Big idea: the liver makes bile, the gallbladder stores it, and the small intestine uses it to emulsify fats.

questions.prompt: Chemical digestion occurs as a result of the action of

choices.explanation: Incorrect by itself. HCl helps, but so do pepsin and saliva.
Incorrect by itself. Pepsin helps, but so do HCl and saliva.
Incorrect by itself. Saliva helps, but so do HCl and pepsin.
Correct. All three take part in chemical digestion.

questions.explanation:
The answer is 'all of the above'. Chemical digestion means breaking food molecules into smaller molecules using chemicals.

Saliva contains amylase to digest starch. Pepsin digests proteins. Hydrochloric acid unfolds proteins and activates pepsin, so it also plays a part in chemical digestion.

Big idea: chemical digestion uses enzymes and other chemicals throughout the digestive tract.

questions.prompt: The first portion of the small intestine is the ______________ .

choices.explanation: Incorrect. The colon is part of the large intestine.
Incorrect. The ileum is the last part of the small intestine.
Correct. The duodenum is the first part of the small intestine.
Incorrect. The rectum is the end of the large intestine.

questions.explanation:
The answer is the duodenum. The small intestine has three parts in order: duodenum, jejunum, and ileum.

The duodenum receives food from the stomach and digestive juices from the pancreas and liver. The colon and rectum are parts of the large intestine.

Big idea: Dow Jones Industrial: Duodenum, Jejunum, Ileum.

questions.prompt: The structure labeled "1" in the diagram below is found in the ______________.

choices.explanation: Incorrect. The kidney has nephrons, not villi.
Incorrect. The esophagus has a smooth lining without villi.
Correct. Villi are found in the small intestine.
Incorrect. The tongue has papillae, not villi.
Incorrect. The heart does not have villi.

questions.explanation:
The answer is the small intestine. Structure 1 is a villus, a finger-like projection of the intestinal lining.

Villi are found only in the small intestine, where they increase the surface area for absorbing nutrients. The kidney, esophagus, tongue, and heart do not have villi.

Big idea: villi are a signature feature of the small intestine.

questions.prompt: What is the name of structure labeled "5" on the diagram below?

choices.explanation: Incorrect. The liver is the large organ on the other side, label 1.
Correct. Label 5 points to the stomach.
Incorrect. The duodenum is the start of the small intestine, below the stomach.
Incorrect. The ileum (spelled 'ilium' here) is the end of the small intestine, lower in the abdomen.
Incorrect. The jejunum is part of the coiled small intestine, lower down.

questions.explanation:
The answer is the stomach. In the diagram, label 5 points to the J-shaped sac on the left side of the upper abdomen, below where the esophagus ends.

The stomach stores food, churns it, and starts protein digestion. The liver is the large organ on the right (label 1), and the duodenum, jejunum, and ileum are parts of the small intestine.

Big idea: knowing where each digestive organ sits in the abdomen helps you identify it in diagrams.

questions.prompt: The second portion of the large intestine is called the ______________________.

choices.explanation: Not this key's answer. The ascending colon is the first section of the colon (it would be second only if you count the cecum first).
Incorrect. The descending colon comes after the transverse colon.
Correct. The transverse colon is the second portion of the colon.
Incorrect. The appendix is a small pouch attached to the cecum.
Incorrect. The cecum is the pouch at the very start of the large intestine.

questions.explanation:
The answer is the transverse colon. The large intestine runs: cecum (with the appendix attached), ascending colon (up the right side), transverse colon (across the top), descending colon (down the left side), sigmoid colon, and rectum.

This key counts only the sections of the colon: ascending first, transverse second. If you count the cecum as the first portion of the large intestine, the ascending colon would be second, so read this question as asking about the colon's sections. The appendix is a small pouch on the cecum, not a portion of the colon.

Big idea: the colon forms a frame around the small intestine: up, across, and down.

questions.prompt: What is the main function of the large intestine?

choices.text: To absorb water and make waste a solid that will exit the body.
choices.explanation: Correct. The large intestine absorbs water and forms solid waste.

choices.text: To chemically digest nutrients secreted from the small intestine.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Chemical digestion is mostly finished in the small intestine.

choices.text: To begin the production of urine.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Urine is made by the kidneys.

choices.text: To mechanically digest nutrients secreted from the small intestine.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Mechanical digestion happens mainly in the mouth and stomach.

choices.text: To regulate the amount of glucose in blood.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Blood sugar is regulated by pancreatic hormones.

questions.explanation:
The answer is to absorb water and make waste solid. By the time material reaches the large intestine, most nutrients have already been absorbed.

The large intestine absorbs water and salts, turning the liquid leftovers into solid stool, which is stored until it leaves the body. It does not make urine (that is the kidneys) or control blood sugar (that is the pancreas).

Big idea: the large intestine's main job is water absorption and forming feces.

questions.prompt: Identify the structure labeled 10 in the diagram.
questions.explanation:
Label 10 is the liver, the large purple organ in the upper right abdomen.

The liver makes bile for fat digestion, processes nutrients from the intestines, stores glycogen, and removes toxins from the blood.

Big idea: the liver is the largest accessory organ of digestion.

questions.prompt: Identify the structure labeled 11 in the diagram.
questions.explanation:
Label 11 is the gallbladder, the small green sac tucked under the liver.

The gallbladder stores and concentrates bile made by the liver, then squeezes it into the duodenum when fatty food arrives.

Big idea: the liver makes bile; the gallbladder stores it.

questions.prompt: Identify the structure labeled 12 in the diagram.
questions.explanation:
Label 12 is the duodenum, the first, C-shaped part of the small intestine, just after the stomach.

The duodenum receives food from the stomach plus bile and pancreatic juice, so most chemical digestion happens here.

Big idea: the small intestine is duodenum, jejunum, then ileum.

questions.prompt: Identify the structure labeled 13 in the diagram.
questions.explanation:
Label 13 is the stomach, the J-shaped sac in the upper left abdomen.

The stomach stores food, churns it with acid and enzymes, and begins protein digestion before passing chyme to the duodenum.

Big idea: the stomach is a muscular mixing and storage organ.

questions.prompt: Identify the structure labeled 14 in the diagram.
questions.explanation:
Label 14 is the pancreas, the long yellowish gland behind the stomach.

The pancreas sends digestive enzymes and bicarbonate into the duodenum, and also releases insulin and glucagon into the blood.

Big idea: the pancreas has both digestive (exocrine) and hormone (endocrine) jobs.

questions.prompt: Identify the structure labeled 15 in the diagram.
questions.explanation:
Label 15 is the jejunum, the middle part of the small intestine, in the upper left part of the coiled intestines.

The jejunum has many folds and tall villi, and it is where most nutrients are absorbed.

Big idea: the jejunum is the main absorbing section of the small intestine.

questions.prompt: Identify the structure labeled 16 in the diagram.
questions.explanation:
Label 16 is the ileum, the last part of the small intestine, in the lower coils.

The ileum absorbs vitamin B12 and bile salts and contains many Peyer's patches. It connects to the cecum of the large intestine.

Big idea: the ileum is the longest and final section of the small intestine.

questions.prompt: Identify the structure labeled 17 in the diagram.
questions.explanation:
Label 17 is the parotid gland, the largest salivary gland, located in front of the ear.

Its duct opens inside the cheek near the upper molars. It makes watery saliva rich in amylase.

Big idea: there are three pairs of major salivary glands: parotid, submandibular, and sublingual.

questions.prompt: Identify the structure labeled 18 in the diagram.
questions.explanation:
Label 18 points to the salivary glands under the jaw and tongue (the submandibular and sublingual glands).

These glands release saliva into the floor of the mouth. Saliva moistens food and starts starch digestion.

Big idea: salivary glands are accessory digestive organs.

questions.prompt: Which enzyme found in the mouth initiates the digestion of carbohydrates?

choices.explanation: Correct. Salivary amylase starts carbohydrate digestion.
Incorrect. Lipase digests fats.
Incorrect. Proteases digest proteins.
Incorrect. Pepsin digests proteins in the stomach.

questions.explanation:
The answer is amylase. Salivary amylase starts breaking starch into smaller sugars in the mouth.

Lipase digests fat, protease digests protein, and pepsin is a protease in the stomach.

Big idea: carbohydrate digestion begins in the mouth with amylase.

questions.prompt: An experiment is conducted where one group is given 60 grams of glucose orally and the other group is given 60 grams of glucose intravenously. Which choice below explains why the intravenous glucose load is cleared at a slower rate from the blood compared to the oral glucose load?

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Glucagon raises blood sugar; it would not clear glucose faster.
Incorrect. VIP does not cause GIP release.
Incorrect. GIP does not work by releasing VIP.
Correct. GIP from the gut causes extra insulin release after oral glucose.

questions.explanation:
The answer is GIP-induced insulin release (the question spells it 'GLIP'). GIP (glucose-dependent insulinotropic peptide) is a hormone made by the small intestine when food, especially glucose, arrives.

GIP tells the pancreas to release extra insulin, so glucose eaten by mouth is cleared from the blood faster. Glucose given straight into a vein skips the intestine, so no GIP is released, less insulin is made, and the glucose stays in the blood longer. This is called the incretin effect.

Big idea: the gut tells the pancreas that food is coming, which helps control blood sugar after a meal.

questions.prompt: A boy eats a hearty meal of 40% carbohydrates, 35% proteins, and 25% fats. At what time after the meal (in hours) will the boy’s gastric juice most likely have the lowest pH?

choices.explanation: Incorrect. At 0.5 hours, lots of food is buffering the acid.
Incorrect. At 1.5 hours, food is still buffering the acid.
Incorrect. At 2.5 hours, some food is still present.
Correct. By 3.5 hours the stomach has mostly emptied, so acid is unbuffered and pH is lowest.

questions.explanation:
The answer is 3.5 hours. Right after a meal, food mixes with stomach acid and acts like a buffer, soaking up acid and keeping the pH from dropping very low.

As the stomach slowly empties its contents into the duodenum over several hours, there is less food left to buffer the acid, but the stomach keeps secreting acid. So the pH of the gastric juice is lowest late, around 3-4 hours after the meal.

Big idea: food buffers stomach acid, so the stomach is most acidic when it is nearly empty.

questions.prompt: Where does the majority of bile salts get absorbed within the digestive tract?

choices.explanation: Incorrect. The esophagus does not absorb bile salts.
Correct. Most bile salts are reabsorbed in the ileum of the small intestine.
Incorrect. Only a small amount reaches the large intestine.
Incorrect. Bile is not released into the stomach.

questions.explanation:
The answer is the small intestine. Bile salts help digest fats in the small intestine. Then about 95% of them are reabsorbed in the last part of the small intestine (the ileum).

The reabsorbed bile salts travel back to the liver to be used again. This recycling loop is called enterohepatic circulation. Very few bile salts reach the large intestine.

Big idea: the body recycles bile salts instead of making new ones each meal.

questions.prompt: What is the innermost layer of the alimentary canal?

choices.explanation: Incorrect. The serosa is the outermost layer.
Incorrect. The submucosa is the second layer.
Correct. The mucosa is the innermost layer.
Incorrect. The muscularis mucosae is a thin muscle layer inside the mucosa, not the innermost layer.

questions.explanation:
The answer is the mucosa. The wall of the alimentary canal has four layers. From the inside (lumen) out: mucosa, submucosa, muscularis externa, and serosa.

The mucosa lines the inside and touches the food. The muscularis mucosae is only a thin part within the mucosa, not a separate innermost layer.

Big idea: Mucosa, Submucosa, Muscularis, Serosa, from inside to outside.

questions.prompt: Under basal conditions, which ion has the highest concentration in saliva?

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Sodium is removed by the ducts, so it is low in saliva.
Incorrect. Chloride is removed by the ducts, so it is low in saliva.
Correct. Duct cells add bicarbonate, which helps neutralize acid in the mouth.
Incorrect for this key. Potassium is also added and is high in saliva, but the key chose bicarbonate.

questions.explanation:
The answer is bicarbonate (per this key). Saliva starts out in the gland similar to blood plasma, but as it flows through the ducts, the duct cells remove sodium and chloride and add potassium and bicarbonate.

Because of this, saliva ends up with less sodium and chloride than blood and more potassium and bicarbonate. The bicarbonate helps neutralize acids in the mouth and protects the teeth. (Exact amounts change with how fast saliva flows, so different textbooks rank potassium and bicarbonate differently.)

Big idea: salivary ducts change the ions in saliva on its way to the mouth.

questions.prompt: An old woman has developed a struggle to swallow food. Her body cannot determine if a bolus of food is big or small enough to be swallowed. Which structure most likely has been impacted?

choices.explanation: Incorrect. The epiglottis covers the airway; it does not judge bolus size.
Correct. The palatopharyngeal folds form a slit that only lets small enough pieces pass.
Incorrect. The upper esophageal sphincter opens to let food into the esophagus, but does not sort it.
Incorrect. The larynx is closed off during swallowing.

questions.explanation:
The answer is the palatopharyngeal folds. These folds of tissue at the sides of the throat come together during swallowing, leaving only a narrow slit.

This slit acts like a sorting gate: only food that is chewed well enough can pass into the lower pharynx, while large pieces are held back. If the folds are damaged, the body cannot judge whether a bolus is the right size. The epiglottis covers the airway, and the upper esophageal sphincter opens to let food into the esophagus, but neither sorts food by size.

Big idea: swallowing involves several structures working in sequence to move food safely.

questions.prompt: Under physiological conditions, which gastrointestinal hormone inhibits gastric emptying?

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Gastrin increases stomach acid and movement.
Incorrect. Motilin increases gut movement between meals.
Incorrect. Secretin can slow emptying a little, but CCK is the main hormone that does this.
Correct. CCK slows gastric emptying when fat reaches the duodenum.

questions.explanation:
The answer is CCK (cholecystokinin). When fats and proteins enter the duodenum, it releases CCK.

CCK slows down how fast the stomach empties, giving the small intestine time to digest the fat. It also makes the gallbladder release bile and the pancreas release enzymes. Gastrin and motilin increase stomach movement. Secretin also slows emptying, but CCK is the main hormone that does this.

Big idea: hormones from the small intestine slow the stomach so the intestine is not overloaded.

questions.prompt: Which mechanism allows transportation of substances across the luminal cell membrane of an enterocyte in infants but not in adults?

choices.explanation: Correct. Infant intestinal cells can absorb whole proteins like antibodies by endocytosis.
Incorrect. Primary active transport works in adults too.
Incorrect. Passive diffusion works in adults too.
Incorrect. Facilitated diffusion works in adults too.

questions.explanation:
The answer is endocytosis. In newborns, cells lining the small intestine can take in whole proteins by wrapping their membrane around them (endocytosis).

This lets babies absorb whole antibodies (like IgG) from breast milk, giving them passive immunity. Adult intestinal cells mostly lose this ability; they absorb small nutrients using diffusion and transport proteins instead.

Big idea: a baby's gut is built to absorb antibodies from milk.

questions.prompt: The stomach is a great absorptive area because it has typical villus type of absorptive membrane.
questions.explanation:
This statement is false. The stomach does not have villi, and it absorbs very little: mainly some water, alcohol, and a few drugs like aspirin.

Its lining is covered with gastric pits and glands that make acid, enzymes, and mucus. Villi are found in the small intestine, which is the main absorbing organ.

Big idea: the stomach digests and stores; the small intestine absorbs.

questions.prompt: This is the wave-like movement of muscles which moves food through the digestive system (one-word)
questions.explanation:
The answer is peristalsis. Peristalsis is a wave of smooth muscle contraction that moves along the digestive tract, pushing food forward.

The muscle behind the food squeezes while the muscle in front relaxes, like squeezing toothpaste through a tube.

Big idea: peristalsis moves food from the esophagus all the way through the intestines.

questions.prompt: This hormone stimulates the stomach to secrete gastric juice and influences the stomach's motor functions (one word)
questions.explanation:
The answer is gastrin. Gastrin is a hormone made by G cells in the stomach when food (especially protein) arrives.

It travels in the blood and tells the stomach to make more acid and gastric juice and to churn more strongly.

Big idea: hormones like gastrin coordinate digestion.

questions.prompt: This enzyme of the stomach is active around a pH of 2.0-3.0 and becomes inactive at above 5.0 (one-word)
questions.explanation:
The answer is pepsin. Pepsin is the stomach's protein-digesting enzyme. It works best in very acidic conditions (pH around 2-3).

When the food moves into the duodenum, bicarbonate raises the pH above 5 and pepsin stops working. The pancreas's protein enzymes take over there.

Big idea: each digestive enzyme works best at a particular pH.

questions.prompt: You prescribe her Omeprazole, a proton-pump inhibitor, to treat her stomach ulcers. Why would a PPI help in this situation?
questions.context: A patient comes in claiming she has burning stomach pain and heartburn. She also claims she’s been overly stressed lately from work and school.
questions.answer: PPIs will reduce the amount of acid produced by cells lining the stomach
questions.explanation:
A proton pump inhibitor (PPI), like omeprazole, blocks the proton pumps in the stomach's parietal cells.

These pumps are what push hydrogen ions into the stomach to make hydrochloric acid. With less acid, the ulcer is not irritated as much, so it can heal, and the burning pain eases.

Big idea: ulcer treatments reduce stomach acid or remove its cause (like H. pylori).

questions.prompt: Additionally, you tell her to take sodium bicarbonate orally in combination with Omeprazole. What is a possible consequence of consuming an excess of sodium bicarbonate?
questions.context: A patient comes in claiming she has burning stomach pain and heartburn. She also claims she’s been overly stressed lately from work and school.
questions.answer: It can result in metabolic alkalosis
questions.explanation:
Taking too much sodium bicarbonate can cause metabolic alkalosis. Sodium bicarbonate is a base (it neutralizes acid). Some of it is absorbed into the blood.

If too much is absorbed, the blood becomes too basic (pH too high). The body responds by breathing more slowly to keep carbon dioxide, which acts as an acid.

Big idea: the body keeps blood pH in a narrow range; the lungs help balance it by changing how much CO2 is breathed out.

questions.prompt: What causes lactose intolerance?
questions.context: A population study was conducted regarding lactose intolerance.
questions.answer: The body is not producing enough lactase to digest lactose
questions.explanation:
Lactose intolerance happens when the body does not make enough lactase, the enzyme in the small intestine that splits lactose (milk sugar) into glucose and galactose.

Undigested lactose travels to the large intestine, where bacteria ferment it, producing gas and pulling in water. This causes bloating, cramps, gas, and diarrhea.

Big idea: missing a digestive enzyme means that food cannot be absorbed and causes symptoms.

questions.prompt: Which population descent has evolutionarily developed lactose tolerance?
questions.context: A population study was conducted regarding lactose intolerance.
questions.explanation:
The answer is people of northern European descent. In most mammals, lactase production drops after weaning (when babies stop drinking milk).

Thousands of years ago, groups that raised dairy animals, especially in northern Europe, developed gene changes that keep lactase working into adulthood (lactase persistence). Being able to digest milk gave them a survival advantage, so the trait became common. Some herding groups in Africa and the Middle East developed it too.

Big idea: lactose tolerance in adults is an example of human evolution linked to diet.

questions.prompt: A patient comes in claiming she’s had chronic nausea for the last four years with occasional vomiting. The physical examination shows no abnormalities. You schedule her for an upper GI endoscopy and find an area of gastric fundal mucosa with a loss of rugal folds. The biopsies that are examined show well-differentiated adenocarcinoma confined to the mucosa. A previous upper GI endoscopy performed four years ago showed microscopic chronic inflammation and a pattern of gastritis. What is the most likely risk factor for her neoplasm?
questions.explanation:
The most likely risk factor is Helicobacter pylori infection. H. pylori is a bacterium that lives in the stomach lining and causes long-term inflammation (chronic gastritis), which this patient had four years earlier.

Years of inflammation can slowly change stomach cells into cancer cells. H. pylori is the strongest known risk factor for stomach adenocarcinoma.

Big idea: long-term infection and inflammation can lead to cancer in the digestive system.

questions.prompt: A man comes in claiming he’s felt extremely fatigued for last three months. The physical examination shows no abnormalities. The laboratory examination shows he has a total protein of 5.3 g/dL, albumin 3.0 g/dL, ALT 133 U/L and AST 113 U/L with total bilirubin 1.2 mg/dL and direct bilirubin 0.7 mg/dL. You perform a liver biopsy and find focal ballooning degeneration of hepatocytes. Your microscopic examination shows surface inflammation with inflammation extending into the lobules from triads. What laboratory test finding is most characteristic of your patient’s disease?
questions.explanation:
The most characteristic finding is a positive hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg). The patient has signs of liver inflammation: high liver enzymes (ALT and AST), low albumin, and inflammation spreading from the portal areas into the liver tissue on biopsy.

These findings fit chronic viral hepatitis. Hepatitis B surface antigen is a protein from the virus's outer coat; finding it in the blood means the person is infected with hepatitis B.

Big idea: hepatitis means liver inflammation, and blood tests for viral proteins identify the cause.

questions.prompt: An obese woman comes in claiming she’s been experiencing abdominal pain and fatigue for the last few months. She has a history of diabetes, hypertension, and hyperlipidemia. The laboratory examination shows elevated liver enzymes, and an x-ray shows an enlarged liver. What is her probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The answer is hepatitis, here a non-alcoholic fatty liver hepatitis (also called NASH or MASH). The woman is obese and has diabetes, high blood pressure, and high blood fats.

These conditions cause fat to build up in the liver. The fat can inflame the liver, raising liver enzymes and enlarging the liver. Fatty liver disease is now one of the most common liver diseases.

Big idea: hepatitis can be caused by viruses, alcohol, or fat buildup linked to obesity.

questions.prompt: Why is pepsin needed to digest meat?
questions.context: A patient comes in claiming that he bloats and has stomach pains when consuming meat. He can still digest meat (proteins) but there is discomfort. You run some tests and find that he lacks pepsin in his stomach.
questions.answer: Pepsin is important for digesting collagen which is a major constituent of intercellular connective tissue of meats.
questions.explanation:
Pepsin is needed because it can digest collagen. Collagen is the tough protein in the connective tissue that holds meat fibers together.

Pepsin breaks down collagen in the stomach so that other enzymes can reach the rest of the meat's proteins. Without pepsin, meat is harder to break apart, so the person can still digest it but feels discomfort.

Big idea: protein digestion begins in the stomach with pepsin, which handles tough proteins like collagen.

questions.prompt: Where does most of the body’s protein digestion occur?
