questions.context: A patient comes in claiming that he bloats and has stomach pains when consuming meat. He can still digest meat (proteins) but there is discomfort. You run some tests and find that he lacks pepsin in his stomach.
questions.answer: Most protein digestion occurs in the upper small intestine (duodenum and jejunum)
questions.explanation:
Most protein digestion happens in the upper small intestine (the duodenum and jejunum).

There, enzymes from the pancreas (like trypsin and chymotrypsin) and enzymes on the intestinal lining break proteins into amino acids, which are then absorbed. The stomach only starts the process.

Big idea: the small intestine is where most digestion of all nutrients happens.

questions.prompt: What type of enzymes influence protein digestion in the digestive structure from the previous question?
questions.context: A patient comes in claiming that he bloats and has stomach pains when consuming meat. He can still digest meat (proteins) but there is discomfort. You run some tests and find that he lacks pepsin in his stomach.
questions.explanation:
The enzymes are proteolytic enzymes (proteases), which break proteins into smaller pieces.

In the small intestine, these include trypsin, chymotrypsin, and carboxypeptidase from the pancreas, and peptidases on the intestinal lining that finish the job by producing single amino acids.

Big idea: 'proteolytic' means 'protein-splitting'.

questions.prompt: Where are these enzymes (previous question) secreted from?
questions.context: A patient comes in claiming that he bloats and has stomach pains when consuming meat. He can still digest meat (proteins) but there is discomfort. You run some tests and find that he lacks pepsin in his stomach.
questions.explanation:
These enzymes are secreted by the pancreas. The pancreas makes them in an inactive form (like trypsinogen) so they do not digest the pancreas itself.

They travel through the pancreatic duct into the duodenum, where they are activated. (A few protein-digesting enzymes also come from the intestinal lining.)

Big idea: the pancreas makes the main digestive enzymes used in the small intestine.

questions.prompt: Stimulation of the sympathetic nervous system will do what to the mucosal muscle?
questions.context: You are running to class and dash across the street. A car almost hits you, frightening you. Your sympathetic nervous system has been activated.
questions.explanation:
The key says sympathetic stimulation excites the muscularis mucosae (the thin muscle layer within the gut lining).

Even though the 'fight or flight' system generally slows digestion, some textbooks (such as Guyton) note that sympathetic nerves can cause the thin muscularis mucosae to contract while the main gut muscles relax. This can change the folds of the lining.

Big idea: the nervous system controls gut muscles, and the sympathetic system's main effect is to slow digestion.

questions.prompt: Stimulation of the sympathetic nervous system will do what to the activity of the GI tract?
questions.context: You are running to class and dash across the street. A car almost hits you, frightening you. Your sympathetic nervous system has been activated.
questions.explanation:
Sympathetic stimulation inhibits (slows) the GI tract. When you are frightened, the 'fight or flight' system sends blood away from the gut to the muscles and heart.

It slows peristalsis, reduces digestive secretions, and tightens the sphincters. Digestion can wait until the danger is over; the parasympathetic 'rest and digest' system speeds it up again.

Big idea: sympathetic = fight or flight (slows digestion); parasympathetic = rest and digest (speeds it up).

questions.prompt: A boy has a hearty meal for lunch. About 50 minutes later, the ileocecal sphincter relaxes and chyme proceeds into the cecum. Which reflex controls the relaxation of the ileocecal sphincter?

choices.explanation: Incorrect. The gastrocolic reflex increases movement in the colon.
Correct. The gastroileal reflex relaxes the ileocecal sphincter after a meal.
Incorrect. The enterogastric reflex slows the stomach.
Incorrect. The rectosphincteric reflex is part of defecation.

questions.explanation:
The answer is the gastroileal reflex. When food enters the stomach, a reflex makes the ileum move more and the ileocecal sphincter relax.

This lets chyme from the end of the small intestine pass into the cecum, making room for the new meal coming behind it. The gastrocolic reflex moves material through the colon, the enterogastric reflex slows the stomach, and the rectosphincteric reflex is involved in defecation.

Big idea: reflexes coordinate movement along the gut so new food can move in as older food moves on.

questions.prompt: Identify the correct sequence of the divisions of the small intestine.

choices.explanation: Incorrect. The duodenum comes first.
Correct. Duodenum, then jejunum, then ileum.
Incorrect. The ileum is last.
Incorrect. This is backwards.
Incorrect. The jejunum comes before the ileum.

questions.explanation:
The answer is duodenum, jejunum, ileum. Food leaving the stomach enters the duodenum first, then the jejunum, then the ileum, which joins the large intestine.

Memory trick: 'Dow Jones Industrial'.

Big idea: the three parts of the small intestine always come in the same order.

questions.prompt: Select ALL accessory digestive organs.

choices.explanation: Correct. Salivary glands are accessory organs that make saliva.
Correct. The gallbladder stores bile and is an accessory organ.
Incorrect. Food travels through the esophagus, so it is part of the alimentary canal.
Incorrect. Food travels through the colon, so it is part of the alimentary canal.
Correct. The liver makes bile and is an accessory organ.

questions.explanation:
The answers are the salivary glands, gallbladder, and liver. Accessory digestive organs help digestion, but food does not travel through them.

Salivary glands make saliva, the liver makes bile, and the gallbladder stores bile. The pancreas is another accessory organ. The esophagus and colon are part of the alimentary canal, the tube food actually passes through.

Big idea: the alimentary canal is the food tube; accessory organs add secretions to it.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is a function of the large intestine?

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Amino acids are absorbed in the small intestine.
Incorrect. Lipid digestion happens in the small intestine.
Incorrect. The bolus is broken down in the mouth and stomach.
Correct. The large intestine absorbs vitamin K made by gut bacteria.
Incorrect. The large intestine absorbs sodium; it does not mainly secrete it.

questions.explanation:
The answer is absorption of vitamin K. Trillions of helpful bacteria live in the large intestine. Some of them make vitamin K, which the large intestine absorbs. Vitamin K is needed for blood clotting.

The large intestine also absorbs water and salts. It does not recycle amino acids, digest fats, or break down the bolus (that happens in the mouth and stomach), and it absorbs sodium rather than secreting it.

Big idea: the large intestine absorbs water, salts, and vitamins made by gut bacteria.

questions.prompt: The inability to digest foods containing lactose often occurs due to the inhibition of what gene?

choices.explanation: Incorrect. LAC is not the human lactase gene.
Correct. LCT is the human gene for lactase.
Incorrect. MCM is a gene involved in copying DNA; one nearby region (MCM6) controls LCT, but LCT itself makes lactase.
Incorrect. DRY is not a real gene for lactase.
Incorrect. lacZ is a bacterial gene, not a human one.

questions.explanation:
The answer is LCT. The LCT gene contains the instructions for making lactase, the enzyme that digests lactose (milk sugar).

In many people, this gene is gradually turned down after childhood, so less lactase is made, causing lactose intolerance. (LacZ is a similar gene in bacteria, not humans.)

Big idea: genes code for enzymes, and less enzyme can mean a food cannot be digested.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is not a pancreatic hormone?

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Glucagon is made by the pancreas's alpha cells.
Incorrect. Amylin is released with insulin by beta cells.
Correct. Peptide YY is made by the intestine, not the pancreas.
Incorrect. Somatostatin is made by the pancreas's delta cells (and other places).
Incorrect. Ghrelin is made mostly by the stomach, but pancreatic epsilon cells also make some.

questions.explanation:
The answer is peptide YY. Peptide YY is made by cells in the small and large intestine (especially the ileum and colon). It is released after eating and helps you feel full.

The pancreatic islets make glucagon (alpha cells), insulin and amylin (beta cells), somatostatin (delta cells), and a small amount of ghrelin (epsilon cells), although most ghrelin comes from the stomach.

Big idea: the pancreas's islets make several hormones, but many gut hormones come from the intestine itself.

questions.prompt: Select ALL structures that are involved in mastication.

choices.explanation: Correct. Bicuspids (premolars) grind food during chewing.
Not counted. The submandibular gland moistens food, but it is not usually counted as a chewing structure.
Incorrect. The pharynx is used for swallowing, not chewing.
Correct. The tongue moves food between the teeth while chewing.
Incorrect. The ampulla of Vater is in the duodenum.

questions.explanation:
The answers are the bicuspids and the tongue. Mastication means chewing. The bicuspids (premolars) are teeth that crush and grind food. The tongue moves food around between the teeth and shapes it into a bolus.

The submandibular gland makes saliva, which moistens food, but it is a gland, not a chewing structure. The pharynx is used in swallowing, not chewing. The ampulla of Vater is where bile and pancreatic juice enter the duodenum.

Big idea: chewing uses teeth, tongue, and jaw muscles to break food into smaller pieces.
questions.note: Uncertain: the submandibular gland (B) moistens food but is not usually counted as a structure of mastication.

questions.prompt: As part of their treatment plan, a patient is recommended to take on a low-residue diet for two weeks. Which of the following conditions does this individual most likely have?

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Lactose intolerance is treated by avoiding lactose, not fiber.
Correct. A short low-residue diet rests the bowel while recovering from appendicitis.
Incorrect. Stomach ulcers are treated by reducing acid and treating H. pylori.
Incorrect. Hepatitis is not treated with a low-residue diet.
Incorrect. Celiac disease is treated with a gluten-free diet.

questions.edited: Option E changed from "Adenocarcinoma" (also a valid indication for a low-residue diet) to "Celiac disease".
questions.explanation:
The answer is appendicitis. A low-residue diet means eating foods with little fiber, so less undigested material (residue) passes through the intestines. This gives the bowel a rest.

Doctors often recommend it for a short time while the intestines heal, such as after surgery for appendicitis. The other conditions need different diets: lactose intolerance (avoid milk sugar), stomach ulcers (avoid irritants), hepatitis (support the liver, avoid alcohol), and celiac disease (avoid gluten).

Big idea: diet is part of the treatment for many digestive diseases, and each disease needs a different change.

questions.prompt: Select ALL substances involved in lipid digestion.

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Chymotrypsin digests proteins.
Correct. Bile salts emulsify fats so they can be digested.
Incorrect. Vitamin B12 is not involved in fat digestion.
Incorrect. Pancreatic polypeptide is a hormone, not a fat-digesting substance.
Incorrect. Acetylcholine is a nerve signal, not part of fat digestion.

questions.explanation:
The answer is bile salts. Bile salts break large fat drops into many tiny droplets (emulsification), giving lipase more surface to work on. They also help carry the digested fats to the intestinal cells for absorption.

Chymotrypsin digests proteins, vitamin B12 is a vitamin, pancreatic polypeptide is a hormone that adjusts pancreatic secretions, and acetylcholine is a nerve signal. None of these directly digests fat.

Big idea: fat digestion needs both bile salts (to emulsify) and lipase (to break the fat molecules apart).

questions.prompt: Which of the following correctly matches the structure to the frequency of its basal electrical rhythm?

choices.explanation: Correct. The stomach's basal electrical rhythm is about 3 per minute.
Incorrect. The duodenum's rhythm is about 12 per minute.
Incorrect. The ileum's rhythm is about 8-9 per minute.
Incorrect. Only the stomach match is right.
Incorrect. The stomach match is correct.

questions.explanation:
The answer is 'Stomach; 3/min'. The basal electrical rhythm (BER) is a slow, wave-like electrical signal in the smooth muscle of the gut that sets the pace of contractions.

In the stomach, it beats about 3 times per minute. In the duodenum it is about 12 per minute, and in the ileum about 8-9 per minute. So only the stomach match is correct.

Big idea: the gut has its own built-in pacemaker rhythm, which is fastest in the duodenum and slowest in the stomach.

questions.prompt: Select ALL reasons for why the stomach does not get digested by itself.

choices.text: Gastric acid is weakly acidic and cannot digest epithelial tissues
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Stomach acid is very strong (pH about 1.5-3.5).

choices.text: A thick layer of bicarbonate-rich mucus covers the lining of the stomach, neutralizing the acid
choices.explanation: Correct. Bicarbonate-rich mucus protects the stomach lining.

choices.text: Stomach epithelium is renewed every few days, so damaged cells are quickly replaced
choices.explanation: Correct. The lining is replaced every few days.

choices.text: Epithelial cells produce a special polypeptide that protects them from the acid
choices.explanation: Incorrect. This statement is too vague; the main protections are mucus, tight junctions, and cell renewal.

choices.text: Tight junctions between epithelial cells seal in gastric acid and regulate permeability of other substances
choices.explanation: Correct. Tight junctions keep acid from seeping between cells.

questions.explanation:
The answers are B, C, and E. The stomach makes very strong acid and protein-digesting enzymes, so it needs protection.

A thick layer of bicarbonate-rich mucus covers the lining and neutralizes acid next to the cells. Tight junctions between cells keep acid from leaking between them. And the lining cells are replaced every few days, so damaged cells do not last. Gastric acid is very strong, not weak. Stomach cells do make some protective proteins, but this choice is too vague to count.

Big idea: the stomach protects itself with mucus, tight seals between cells, and fast cell replacement.

questions.prompt: An experiment uses an in vitro model of the gastric glands. When a particular substance is applied to the culture, the pH of the model increases, while the ATP consumption decreases. Which cell type does this substance primarily affect?

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Chief cells make pepsinogen, not acid.
Correct. Blocking parietal cells' acid pumps raises pH and lowers ATP use.
Incorrect. Foveolar cells make protective mucus.
Incorrect. Enterochromaffin-like cells make histamine, which signals parietal cells, but they do not make acid themselves.
Incorrect. G cells make the hormone gastrin.

questions.explanation:
The answer is parietal cells. Parietal cells make stomach acid using a pump (the proton pump, or H+/K+ ATPase) that uses ATP for energy to push hydrogen ions into the stomach.

If a substance blocks parietal cells, less acid is made, so the pH goes up (less acidic), and less ATP is used by the pumps. That is exactly what the experiment shows. Proton pump inhibitor drugs work this way.

Big idea: making stomach acid takes energy, and blocking parietal cells lowers acid production.

questions.prompt: Which of the following processes begin to occur upon the sight of food?

choices.text: Parasympathetic signals are sent from the hypothalamus to the stomach by the glossopharyngeal nerve
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Signals to the stomach travel through the vagus nerve, not the glossopharyngeal nerve.

choices.text: The duodenum secretes secretin and cholecystokinin, stimulating gastric activity
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Secretin and CCK are released after food reaches the duodenum.

choices.text: Blood rushes through the hepatic portal vein to the liver sinusoids
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Blood flow to the liver increases after eating, not just from seeing food.

choices.text: The superior and inferior salivary nuclei in the pons and medulla are activated, stimulating saliva production
choices.explanation: Correct. Seeing food activates the salivary nuclei and starts saliva flow.

choices.text: Beta cells in the Islets of Langerhans produce large amounts of glucagon
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Beta cells make insulin, not glucagon.

questions.explanation:
The answer is D. Seeing food starts the cephalic phase of digestion. Signals from the brain activate the salivary nuclei in the brainstem (pons and medulla), which make the salivary glands release saliva. Your mouth 'waters'.

The brain also sends signals through the vagus nerve (not the glossopharyngeal nerve) to the stomach. Secretin and CCK are released only after food reaches the duodenum, extra blood flows to the gut after eating, and beta cells make insulin, not glucagon.

Big idea: digestion begins before food even reaches the mouth, triggered by sight, smell, and thought.

questions.prompt: An obstruction of the Stensen’s ducts would prevent the drainage of the contents of what structure?

choices.explanation: Correct. Stensen's duct drains the parotid gland.
Incorrect. The pancreas drains through the pancreatic duct.
Incorrect. The gallbladder drains through the cystic and common bile ducts.
Incorrect. The stomach does not have a duct like this.
Incorrect. Brunner's glands release mucus directly into the duodenum.

questions.explanation:
The answer is the parotid gland. Stensen's duct (the parotid duct) carries saliva from the parotid gland, in front of the ear, across the cheek to open inside the mouth near the upper second molar.

If it is blocked (for example by a stone), saliva backs up and the parotid gland swells. The pancreas and gallbladder drain into the duodenum, and Brunner's glands are in the duodenum's wall.

Big idea: each salivary gland has its own duct; Stensen's duct belongs to the parotid gland.

questions.prompt: A transverse section of the esophagus is prepared. Identify the correct sequence of structures that would be encountered by the sectioning blade.

choices.explanation: Incorrect. This lists the layers from the inside out, and the esophagus mostly has adventitia, not serosa.

choices.text: Longitudinal esophageal muscle, phrenoesophageal ligament, supradiaphragmatic fascia
choices.explanation: Incorrect. These are not the layers of the esophageal wall.
Correct. From outside to inside: adventitia, muscularis, submucosa, mucosa.

choices.text: Circular esophageal muscle, Schatzki ring, cardiac notch, adventitia
choices.explanation: Incorrect. These are not the wall layers in order.

choices.text: Muscularis, infradiaphragmatic fascia, Z line, hyaline cartilage
choices.explanation: Incorrect. The esophagus does not contain hyaline cartilage, and this is not the layer order.

questions.explanation:
The answer is adventitia, muscularis, submucosa, mucosa. A blade cutting into the esophagus from the outside would pass through its layers from outside to inside.

Most of the esophagus is covered on the outside by adventitia (connective tissue) instead of serosa, because it runs through the chest, not the abdomen. Then come the muscularis (muscle), the submucosa, and finally the mucosa that lines the inside.

Big idea: the gut wall's four layers (mucosa, submucosa, muscularis, serosa/adventitia) are the same in order; only the outermost layer's name changes.

questions.prompt: Which of the following correctly matches the structure with its epithelial lining? Select ALL that apply.

choices.explanation: Correct. The mouth is lined with stratified squamous epithelium.
Incorrect. The esophagus is lined with stratified squamous epithelium.
Correct. The stomach is lined with simple columnar epithelium.
Not counted. Bile ducts in the liver have simple cuboidal lining, but the liver itself has no lining, so this is debatable.
Incorrect. The ileum is lined with simple columnar epithelium.

questions.explanation:
The answers are 'oral cavity; stratified squamous' and 'stomach; simple columnar'. The mouth is lined by stratified squamous epithelium, many layers of flat cells that resist scraping from food. The stomach is lined by simple columnar epithelium, a single layer of tall cells that make mucus.

The esophagus is also stratified squamous, not stratified columnar. The ileum is lined with simple columnar cells, not pseudostratified squamous (which is not a real type). The liver's bile ducts are lined with simple cuboidal cells, but the liver itself is not a hollow organ with a lining, so this match is debatable and not counted here.

Big idea: areas that face rubbing have layered, flat cells; areas that absorb or secrete have single layers of tall cells.
questions.note: Uncertain: D (liver; simple cuboidal) is defensible for the bile ducts, but the liver has no luminal lining in the usual sense.

questions.prompt: Select ALL mechanisms by which obesity may negatively affect the gastrointestinal system.

choices.text: The length of the lower esophageal sphincter is shortened
choices.explanation: Correct. Abdominal pressure can shorten the lower esophageal sphincter, causing reflux.

choices.text: The gastrocolic reflex is inhibited and colonic motility is reduced
choices.explanation: Not counted. Evidence about obesity and the gastrocolic reflex is mixed.

choices.text: Firmicutes dominates the gut microbiota and butyrate production declines
choices.explanation: Not counted. Gut bacteria changes with obesity are real but complicated; this exact claim is not clearly established.

choices.text: Basal metabolic rate is significantly decreased
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Basal metabolic rate is about whole-body metabolism, not the digestive system.

choices.text: Abdominal visceral fat produces inflammatory cytokines such as interleukin-6 and tumor necrosis factor
choices.explanation: Correct. Visceral fat releases inflammatory chemicals.

questions.explanation:
The answers are A and E. Obesity raises pressure in the abdomen, which pushes on the stomach and can shorten and weaken the lower esophageal sphincter. This lets acid flow back up, causing GERD (heartburn).

Fat around the abdominal organs (visceral fat) is active tissue that releases inflammatory chemicals like interleukin-6 and TNF, which can harm the liver and gut. The research on choices B and C is mixed, and choice D is about overall metabolism, not the digestive system.

Big idea: obesity affects the digestive system mechanically (pressure) and chemically (inflammation).
questions.note: Uncertain: the evidence for B and C is mixed, and D is not a gastrointestinal effect.

questions.prompt: Irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) is a gastrointestinal condition characterized by symptoms such as abdominal cramping, diarrhea, constipation, bloating, and gas. At which of the following structures would you expect gas accumulation to be most common?

choices.explanation: Incorrect. The ileocecal valve controls flow into the large intestine.
Incorrect. Omental appendices are small fatty pouches on the outside of the colon.
Incorrect. The pyloric sphincter is between the stomach and duodenum.
Incorrect. The valves of Kerckring are folds in the small intestine.
Correct. Gas often gets trapped at the high, sharp splenic flexure.

questions.explanation:
The answer is the splenic flexure. The splenic flexure is the sharp bend in the colon near the spleen, high on the left side, where the transverse colon turns down into the descending colon.

Gas rises and tends to get trapped at this high, sharp bend, causing pain on the upper left side ('splenic flexure syndrome'), which is common in IBS. The ileocecal valve and pyloric sphincter are valves, omental appendices are small fat pouches on the colon, and the valves of Kerckring are folds in the small intestine.

Big idea: the shape of the colon affects where gas collects.

questions.prompt: A sample of intestinal juice is observed to contain high concentrations of zymogens, including pepsinogen, chymotrypsinogen, and proelastase. The function of which of the following enzymes has most likely been affected?

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Carboxypeptidase is one of the enzymes that gets activated, not the starter.
Correct. Enterokinase activates trypsin, which then activates the other zymogens.
Incorrect. Kallikrein is not part of digestive enzyme activation.
Incorrect. Elastase is activated by trypsin; it does not start the chain.
Incorrect. Duodenase is not the main activator.

questions.explanation:
The answer is enterokinase. Many protein-digesting enzymes are made in an inactive form (zymogens) so they do not digest the organs that make them.

In the duodenum, the brush-border enzyme enterokinase (also called enteropeptidase) activates trypsinogen into trypsin. Trypsin then activates the other zymogens, like chymotrypsinogen and proelastase. If enterokinase is not working, these zymogens stay inactive and build up. (Pepsinogen is normally activated by stomach acid.)

Big idea: digestive enzymes are switched on in a chain, and enterokinase starts the chain in the intestine.

questions.prompt: An individual is found to have several sessile serrated polyps in their colon. Select ALL statements that are true of this condition.

choices.explanation: Incorrect. They are pre-cancerous, not cancerous.

choices.text: They are smaller than hyperplastic polyps
choices.explanation: Incorrect. They are usually larger than hyperplastic polyps.

choices.text: They generally occur on the right side of the colon
choices.explanation: Correct. They are most common in the right side of the colon.

choices.text: They are difficult to identify endoscopically
choices.explanation: Correct. Their flat shape makes them hard to spot during colonoscopy.

choices.text: They are significantly more common in men than women
choices.explanation: Incorrect. They are not significantly more common in men.

questions.explanation:
The answers are that they usually occur on the right side of the colon and are difficult to see during endoscopy. Sessile serrated polyps (also called lesions) are flat growths with a saw-tooth pattern under the microscope.

They are pre-cancerous: they are not cancer yet, but they can turn into colorectal cancer over time, so doctors remove them. They are often larger than hyperplastic polyps, are mostly found in the right (ascending) colon, and are flat and pale, so they are easy to miss. They are not much more common in men.

Big idea: colorectal cancer screening finds and removes pre-cancerous polyps before they become cancer.

questions.prompt: Identify the structures depicted in the image.
questions.explanation:
The structures are villi of the small intestine. In the image, the lining forms many tall, finger-like projections that stick up into the inside of the intestine.

Each villus is covered with absorbing cells and has blood capillaries and a lacteal (lymph vessel) in its center. Villi are found only in the small intestine.

Big idea: villi are the small intestine's signature structure for absorbing nutrients.

questions.prompt: What purpose do these structures serve? Name two other structures of the gastrointestinal tract that serve a similar function.
questions.answer: Villi increase the surface area for absorption (and carry brush-border enzymes). Other structures with a similar function: plicae circulares (circular folds) and microvilli.
questions.explanation:
Villi increase the surface area of the small intestine so it can absorb more nutrients. Their surface cells also carry brush-border enzymes that finish digesting food.

Two other structures with a similar job are the plicae circulares (large circular folds of the intestinal wall) and the microvilli (tiny projections on each absorbing cell). Together, folds, villi, and microvilli make the small intestine's absorbing surface enormous.

Big idea: the body increases surface area to speed up absorption, just as the lungs use alveoli for gas exchange.

questions.prompt: Identify the white dots surrounding the structures in question #56.
questions.explanation:
The white dots are goblet cells. Goblet cells make mucus. In this kind of stain, their mucus-filled insides look pale, so they appear as white dots scattered among the absorbing cells.

Their mucus coats and protects the intestinal lining and helps material slide along.

Big idea: the intestinal lining contains absorbing cells and mucus-making goblet cells.

questions.prompt: How would the amount of “white dots” change between the duodenum and colon (in the caudal direction)? What other feature of the intestines also follows this pattern?
questions.answer: Goblet cells increase in number from the duodenum toward the colon. The gut bacterial population (and lymphoid tissue such as Peyer's patches toward the ileum) also increases distally.
questions.explanation:
Goblet cells (the white dots) become more and more common moving from the duodenum toward the colon. The colon has the most, because its contents become more solid and need more mucus to slide along and to protect the lining.

Another feature that also increases toward the end of the intestines is the number of gut bacteria: there are few in the duodenum and huge numbers in the colon. (Lymphoid tissue such as Peyer's patches also increases toward the ileum.) This second part has more than one acceptable answer.

Big idea: the intestinal lining changes along its length to match changing contents and jobs.
questions.note: Uncertain: the second part has several acceptable answers.

questions.prompt: A child has a congenital defect in the epithelium of the structures in question #56, resulting in permanent atrophy. Predict how normal digestive processes would be altered in this condition, and name three examples of symptoms you could expect to see.
questions.answer: Villous atrophy drastically reduces absorptive surface area and brush-border enzyme activity, so digestion and absorption of nutrients (especially fats, carbohydrates, iron, fat-soluble vitamins) are impaired, causing malabsorption. Symptoms: chronic diarrhea, steatorrhea, weight loss/failure to thrive, bloating, dehydration, anemia, vitamin deficiencies.
questions.explanation:
If the villi shrink away (atrophy), the small intestine loses most of its absorbing surface and many of its brush-border enzymes. Food would not be fully digested, and nutrients would not be absorbed well. This is called malabsorption.

Expected symptoms include chronic diarrhea, greasy stools from unabsorbed fat (steatorrhea), weight loss or failure to grow, bloating, dehydration, and deficiencies such as anemia (low iron) or low vitamins A, D, E, and K.

Big idea: villi are essential for absorption, so damage to them (as in celiac disease) causes malabsorption.

questions.prompt: Propose a treatment plan to relieve this child’s condition. Please be specific.
questions.answer: Parenteral nutrition (IV) with fluid and electrolyte replacement, vitamin/mineral supplementation, and evaluation for intestinal transplantation if the atrophy is permanent.
questions.explanation:
Because this child's villi are permanently damaged, eating alone cannot provide enough nutrition. A good plan is to give nutrition directly into the blood through an IV (parenteral nutrition), along with fluids, electrolytes, vitamins, and minerals.

Doctors would also treat diarrhea and dehydration, and, if the damage is permanent, consider an intestinal transplant. This is an open-ended question, so other reasonable, specific plans can also earn credit.

Big idea: when the gut cannot absorb nutrients, nutrition must be delivered another way.
questions.note: Uncertain: open-ended management question.

questions.prompt: Name the processes that are being described. a) Small, localization contractions of the gastrointestinal tract that function to break up or mix its contents, as opposed to propelling them forward. b) Gas exchange that can occur in the rectum, especially in hypoxic conditions.
questions.answer: a) Segmentation; b) enteral ventilation (intestinal/anal respiration)
questions.explanation:
a) The answer is segmentation. Segmentation is when rings of muscle in separate spots squeeze and relax back and forth. This chops and mixes food with digestive juices without pushing it forward much (unlike peristalsis, which moves food along).

b) This describes enteral ventilation, also called intestinal or anal respiration. Some animals, like certain fish and loaches, can absorb oxygen through their intestine. Scientists have experimented with delivering oxygen through the rectum in mammals with low oxygen levels. There is no single standard name, so this part is uncertain.

Big idea: the gut's muscles mix food (segmentation) and move it (peristalsis).
questions.note: Uncertain: part b refers to experimental gas exchange via the rectum, which has no single standard name.

questions.prompt: What is jaundice, and how does it occur?
questions.answer: Jaundice is yellowing of the skin and sclera caused by accumulation of bilirubin. It occurs when bilirubin production exceeds clearance: excess red-cell breakdown (pre-hepatic), liver dysfunction (hepatic), or blocked bile flow (post-hepatic/obstructive).
questions.explanation:
Jaundice is a yellow color of the skin and the whites of the eyes. It happens when bilirubin, a yellow waste product, builds up in the blood.

Bilirubin comes from breaking down hemoglobin in old red blood cells. The liver processes it and sends it out in bile. Jaundice happens when (1) red blood cells are destroyed too quickly, (2) the liver is damaged and cannot process bilirubin (as in hepatitis), or (3) bile flow is blocked (for example by gallstones or a tumor).

Big idea: jaundice is a sign that something is wrong with red blood cell breakdown, the liver, or bile flow.

questions.prompt: Upon performing a blood test on a jaundiced patient, a physician finds elevated levels of alanine aminotransferase (ALT) and aspartate aminotransferase (AST), but normal blood alcohol. Identify the agent of disease and the organ that it affects.
questions.answer: A hepatitis virus (viral hepatitis); the organ affected is the liver.
questions.explanation:
The agent is most likely a hepatitis virus, and the organ affected is the liver. ALT and AST are enzymes found inside liver cells. When liver cells are damaged, these enzymes leak into the blood, so high levels mean liver injury.

Normal blood alcohol makes alcohol-related liver disease less likely. Combined with jaundice, this points to viral hepatitis, an inflammation of the liver caused by a virus.

Big idea: blood tests can show liver damage, and the pattern helps find the cause.

questions.prompt: As lack of appetite is a commonly observed symptom, patients may be provided with a nasogastric tube for adequate nutrition in more severe cases. How are carbohydrates and triglycerides able to be digested when the tube bypasses the site of salivary amylases and lingual lipases?
questions.answer: Digestion is completed in the small intestine: pancreatic amylase digests carbohydrates and pancreatic lipase (with bile salts) digests triglycerides, and brush-border enzymes finish carbohydrate digestion, so salivary and lingual enzymes are not essential.
questions.explanation:
A nasogastric tube delivers food straight into the stomach, skipping the mouth. Salivary amylase and lingual lipase start digestion in the mouth, but they only do a small part of the job.

Most carbohydrate and fat digestion happens in the small intestine. Pancreatic amylase digests starch, brush-border enzymes finish breaking down sugars, and pancreatic lipase (helped by bile salts) digests triglycerides. So the food can still be fully digested.

Big idea: the small intestine, with help from the pancreas and liver, does most chemical digestion.

questions.prompt: If left untreated, fibrosis of the affected organ may occur. At this stage of disease, digestion of what class of type of macromolecule is most likely affected? Explain.
questions.answer: Lipids. Liver fibrosis/cirrhosis reduces bile production and secretion, so fats cannot be emulsified, which impairs fat digestion and absorption (and of fat-soluble vitamins).
questions.explanation:
The most affected macromolecules would be lipids (fats). Long-term liver damage causes scarring (fibrosis and cirrhosis), and a scarred liver makes less bile.

Bile salts are needed to emulsify fats, breaking them into small droplets that lipase can digest, and to help absorb them. With less bile, fat is poorly digested and absorbed, along with the fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E, and K.

Big idea: the liver supports digestion mainly by making bile for fat digestion.

questions.prompt: True or false: Of all types of hepatitis, there is only a vaccine available for hepatitis B.
questions.explanation:
This statement is false. There are vaccines for both hepatitis A and hepatitis B, and many people get both.

The hepatitis B vaccine also protects against hepatitis D, because hepatitis D can only infect people who have hepatitis B. China has also approved a hepatitis E vaccine. There is no vaccine yet for hepatitis C.

Big idea: vaccines are an important way to prevent viral hepatitis.

questions.prompt: Which of the following molecules are absorbed via direct diffusion into intestinal cells?

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Amino acids need carrier proteins.
Incorrect. Monosaccharides need carrier proteins.
Incorrect. Polysaccharides are too large and must be digested first.
Correct. Fatty acids diffuse directly across the cell membrane.
Incorrect. Nucleic acids must be digested before absorption.

questions.explanation:
The answer is fatty acids. Fatty acids are made from fat digestion. Because they dissolve in the fats of cell membranes, they can diffuse directly into intestinal cells.

Amino acids and monosaccharides need transport proteins to get into cells. Polysaccharides and nucleic acids are too large; they must be digested first.

Big idea: fat-soluble substances can cross membranes easily; water-soluble ones need carriers.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is an accessory organ of the digestive system?

choices.explanation: Incorrect by itself. Teeth are accessory organs, but so are the others.
Incorrect by itself. The gallbladder is an accessory organ, but so are the others.
Incorrect by itself. The pancreas is an accessory organ, but so are the others.
Incorrect. Teeth are also accessory organs.
Correct. Teeth, gallbladder, and pancreas are all accessory digestive organs.

questions.explanation:
The answer is 'All of the above'. Accessory digestive organs help digestion but are not part of the tube that food passes through, or (like the teeth) they sit along it and help break food down.

Teeth chew food, the gallbladder stores bile, and the pancreas makes enzymes and bicarbonate. Many textbooks list the teeth, tongue, salivary glands, liver, gallbladder, and pancreas as accessory organs.

Big idea: the alimentary canal is the food tube; accessory organs help from the side.

questions.prompt: A needle entering from the skin to the inside of the digestive canal would pass through layers of tissue in which of the following orders?

choices.explanation: Official answer. These are the right layers, but listed inside-out; a needle from the skin would go the opposite way.
Incorrect. The serosa is not next to the mucosa.
This is identical to A; the key only marks A.
Incorrect. This order mixes up the layers.
Incorrect. This order mixes up the layers.

questions.note: Options A and C are identical, and both list the layers from the lumen outward (the reverse of the path described). The official key is A.
questions.explanation:
The official answer is A, but this question has a problem. A needle going from the skin into the digestive canal would pass through the layers from the OUTSIDE in: serosa, muscularis externa, submucosa, and finally mucosa.

Choices A and C are identical and list the layers from the inside out (mucosa first), which is the reverse of the needle's path. No choice lists the correct outside-in order. Still, A lists the right four layers in the right sequence, just backwards.

Big idea: the gut wall layers from inside to outside are mucosa, submucosa, muscularis externa, and serosa.

questions.prompt: Most digestive epithelium is simple columnar with the exception of epithelia found in the esophagus. What is the primary reason for this difference?

choices.text: To increase surface area for esophageal digestion
choices.explanation: Incorrect. The esophagus does not digest food.

choices.text: To increase the concentration of aquaporins in the area
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Aquaporins are water channels; this is not the reason.

choices.text: To protect the esophagus against abrasion
choices.explanation: Correct. Stratified squamous cells protect against scraping from food.
Incorrect. Neither A nor B is the reason.
Incorrect. Only protection against abrasion is the reason.

questions.explanation:
The answer is to protect the esophagus against abrasion. The esophagus is lined with stratified squamous epithelium, which has many layers of flat cells.

Food that has just been swallowed can be rough and scratchy. Layered cells can wear away on top while new cells replace them from below. The rest of the digestive tract uses simple columnar cells, which are good at absorbing and secreting but would be damaged by scraping. The esophagus does not digest or absorb much.

Big idea: tissues that face wear and tear have many layers of cells.

questions.prompt: Which of the following statements is false regarding the enteric nervous system?

choices.text: It consists of the submucosal and myenteric plexuses
choices.explanation: Incorrect (this is true). The ENS consists of the submucosal and myenteric plexuses.

choices.text: It is located in the esophagus, stomach, and intestines
choices.explanation: Incorrect (this is true). The ENS is found throughout the digestive tract.

choices.text: It contains more neurons than the spinal cord
choices.explanation: Incorrect (this is true). It has more neurons than the spinal cord.

choices.text: It can function independently of the CNS
choices.explanation: Incorrect (this is true). It can work without the brain.

choices.text: It is controlled entirely by the PNS
choices.explanation: Correct (this is false). The ENS can work independently; it is not entirely controlled from outside.

questions.explanation:
The false statement is E: the enteric nervous system is NOT controlled entirely by the peripheral nervous system. The enteric nervous system is the gut's own network of nerves, sometimes called the 'second brain'.

It is made of the submucosal and myenteric plexuses, runs from the esophagus to the anus, contains more neurons than the spinal cord, and can work on its own, although the brain can adjust it through the vagus and sympathetic nerves.

Big idea: the gut can control much of its own activity.

questions.prompt: Obesity results in increased abdominal fat in which intestinal structure?

choices.explanation: Correct. Mesenteries store much of the extra abdominal fat.
Incorrect. Plexi are networks of nerves.
Incorrect. The lumen is the inside space of the intestine.
Incorrect. The omenta also store fat, but the key's answer is the mesenteries.
Incorrect. The jejunum is part of the small intestine, not a fat store.

questions.explanation:
The answer is the mesenteries. The mesentery is a fan-shaped sheet of tissue that holds the intestines to the back wall of the abdomen. It contains blood vessels, lymph vessels, nerves, and fat.

With obesity, a lot of extra fat (visceral fat) is stored in the mesentery, and also in the omenta. This visceral fat releases inflammatory chemicals and is linked to health problems.

Big idea: obesity affects the digestive system partly through fat stored around the intestines.

questions.prompt: Which of the following nutrients can be absorbed without digestion?

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Polypeptides must be broken into amino acids first.
Correct. Cholesterol is absorbed without being digested.
Incorrect for this key. Fatty acids are absorbed directly, but they come from digesting fats.
Incorrect. Oligosaccharides must be broken into simple sugars first.
Incorrect. Cholesterol can be absorbed without digestion.

questions.explanation:
The answer is cholesterol. Cholesterol is already a small molecule that the intestine can absorb as it is, with the help of bile salts.

Polypeptides and oligosaccharides must be broken down into amino acids and simple sugars first. (Fatty acids are absorbed directly too, but they are the end product of fat digestion, so this key counts cholesterol as the nutrient that needs no digestion.)

Big idea: large nutrients must be digested into small units before absorption; some small molecules are absorbed as they are.

questions.prompt: Lin is brushing their teeth. Which part of their buccal cavity would the toothbrush be located in?

choices.explanation: Incorrect. A frenulum is a small fold of tissue, like the one under the tongue.
Correct. The vestibule is the space between the teeth and cheeks/lips.
Incorrect. The fauces is the opening from the mouth into the throat.
Incorrect. The uvula hangs from the soft palate.
Incorrect. The palate is the roof of the mouth.

questions.explanation:
The answer is the vestibule. The vestibule of the mouth is the space between your teeth and gums on one side and your lips and cheeks on the other.

When you brush the outside surfaces of your teeth, the toothbrush is in the vestibule. The frenulum is a small fold of tissue, the fauces is the opening to the throat, the uvula hangs from the soft palate, and the palate is the roof of the mouth.

Big idea: the mouth (buccal cavity) has named regions, and the vestibule is between the teeth and cheeks.

questions.prompt: The reason we need to carefully brush our teeth is so we can remove debris from our ______.

choices.explanation: Incorrect. The root canal is inside the tooth and cannot be brushed.
Incorrect. The root is below the gums and bone.
Incorrect. The periodontal ligament holds the tooth in the bone.
Incorrect. Enamel is the surface being brushed, but the debris hides in the gingival sulcus.
Correct. The gingival sulcus is the groove where debris collects.

questions.explanation:
The answer is the gingival sulcus. The gingival sulcus is the small groove between the tooth and the gum.

Food and bacteria collect there and form plaque. If not cleaned out, they can cause gum disease (gingivitis). Brushing and flossing remove debris from this groove.

Big idea: taking care of the mouth, the start of the digestive tract, prevents disease.

questions.prompt: Which of the following statements is false regarding the cells of the teeth?

choices.text: Dentin is located in the crown
choices.explanation: Incorrect (this is true). Dentin is found in the crown under the enamel.

choices.text: Cementum is located in the root
choices.explanation: Incorrect (this is true). Cementum covers the root.
Also false, but not marked by the key. Odontoblasts make dentin; cementoblasts make cementum.

choices.text: Repair of damaged enamel is slow but possible
choices.explanation: Correct (per the key). Enamel has no cells, so it cannot repair itself.
Incorrect (this is true). Mature enamel contains no cells.

questions.note: Uncertain: statement C ("odontoblasts produce cementum") is also false, since cementoblasts make cementum; the official key only marks D.
questions.explanation:
The official answer is D. Repair of damaged enamel is NOT possible, because enamel has no living cells. The cells that made enamel (ameloblasts) disappear once the tooth comes in, so a cavity in enamel cannot heal on its own.

However, statement C is also false: cementum is made by cementoblasts, while odontoblasts make dentin. So this question actually has two false statements. The true statements are that dentin is in the crown (under the enamel), cementum covers the root, and enamel has no cells.

Big idea: each tooth layer is made by its own type of cell, and enamel cannot regrow.

questions.prompt: What structure in the tooth has a rich supply of nerves, blood, and lymphatic vessels?

choices.explanation: Incorrect. The neck is the area where the crown meets the root.
Incorrect. Cementum is a hard layer covering the root.
Incorrect. Enamel is the hard outer layer with no nerves or vessels.
Correct. The pulp contains nerves, blood vessels, and lymphatic vessels.
Incorrect. Dentin is a hard layer around the pulp.

questions.explanation:
The answer is the pulp cavity. The pulp is the soft, living center of a tooth.

It contains blood vessels that nourish the tooth, nerves that sense pain and temperature, and lymphatic vessels. That is why a deep cavity that reaches the pulp hurts. Enamel, dentin, and cementum are hard, mineralized layers.

Big idea: the tooth's hard layers protect a living core, the pulp.

questions.prompt: You are reading Saladin’s Anatomy & Physiology: The Unity of Form and Function to an 8-month old baby when they begin to smile. You immediately recognize that they are showing off their:

choices.explanation: Correct. Babies' first teeth are deciduous (baby) teeth.
Incorrect. Permanent teeth start coming in around age 6.
Incorrect. 'Evergreen teeth' is not a real term.
Incorrect. Wisdom teeth come in during the late teens or twenties.
Incorrect. 'Greenstick' describes a type of bone fracture, not a tooth.

questions.explanation:
The answer is deciduous teeth. Deciduous teeth are the 'baby teeth' (primary teeth). The first ones usually appear around 6-10 months of age, so an 8-month-old baby may be showing them.

Children have 20 deciduous teeth, which are later replaced by 32 permanent teeth. Wisdom teeth come in much later, and 'evergreen' and 'greenstick' are not types of teeth.

Big idea: humans have two sets of teeth: deciduous and permanent.

questions.prompt: These salivary glands release secretions at a constant rate, keeping the mouth moist even when not eating.

choices.explanation: Incorrect by itself. Lingual glands do this, but so do the others.
Incorrect by itself. Labial glands do this, but so do the others.
Incorrect by itself. Palatine glands do this, but so do the others.
Incorrect by itself. Buccal glands do this, but so do the others.
Correct. All of these minor salivary glands keep the mouth moist.

questions.explanation:
The answer is 'All of the above'. Besides the three big pairs of salivary glands, the mouth has many small (minor) salivary glands in the tongue (lingual), lips (labial), palate (palatine), and cheeks (buccal).

These small glands release saliva slowly all the time, keeping the mouth moist even when you are not eating. The big glands release large amounts mostly when food is present.

Big idea: saliva keeps the mouth moist and starts digestion.

questions.prompt: Which of the following stimuli does not cause an increase in salivation?

choices.text: Sensing the flavor of foods by the taste buds
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Tasting food increases salivation.

choices.text: The smell of food from olfactory receptors
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Smelling food increases salivation.

choices.text: The sight of food in a picture
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Seeing food, even in a picture, can increase salivation.

choices.text: Spicy foods present in the pharynx
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Spicy food in the pharynx increases salivation.

choices.text: Significantly heightened sympathetic nervous system activation
choices.explanation: Correct. Strong sympathetic activation decreases saliva (dry mouth).

questions.explanation:
The answer is strongly heightened sympathetic nervous system activation. The sympathetic 'fight or flight' system reduces watery saliva, which is why your mouth feels dry when you are very nervous.

Tasting food, smelling food, seeing pictures of food, and spicy food in the throat all increase saliva through the parasympathetic 'rest and digest' system.

Big idea: parasympathetic signals increase saliva; strong sympathetic signals decrease it.

questions.prompt: The intersection of the digestive and respiratory systems is found at the:

choices.explanation: Incorrect. The larynx carries only air.
Correct. The pharynx carries both air and food.
Incorrect. The esophagus carries only food.
Incorrect. The palate separates the mouth from the nasal cavity.
Incorrect. The trachea carries only air.

questions.explanation:
The answer is the pharynx. The pharynx (throat) is the passage shared by both systems: air goes through it to the larynx, and food goes through it to the esophagus.

The larynx and trachea carry only air, the esophagus carries only food, and the palate is the roof of the mouth.

Big idea: the pharynx is where the respiratory and digestive pathways cross.

questions.prompt: I am chewing on a sandwich while studying anatomy. I choose to swallow the bite I am eating, which is an example of the:

choices.explanation: Correct. The oral phase is the voluntary part of swallowing.
Incorrect. The pharyngeal phase is an automatic reflex.
Incorrect. The esophageal phase is automatic peristalsis.
Incorrect. There is no tracheal phase of swallowing.
Incorrect. Only the oral phase is the voluntary choice to swallow.

questions.explanation:
The answer is the oral phase of swallowing. Swallowing has three phases. The oral (buccal) phase is voluntary: you choose to push the chewed food to the back of your mouth with your tongue.

Once the food touches the back of the throat, the pharyngeal and esophageal phases happen automatically as reflexes. There is no 'tracheal phase', since food should never enter the trachea.

Big idea: swallowing starts voluntarily and then becomes automatic.

questions.prompt: You are able to swallow while upside-down (don’t try this) because of which of the following actions?

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Covering the airway keeps food out of the lungs but does not move it.
Correct. Peristaltic waves push food down even against gravity.

choices.text: Changes in pressure from the oral cavity to the gut
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Pressure changes are not what move food down the esophagus.

choices.text: Lack of air in the digestive tract, meaning that food cannot fall back out
choices.explanation: Incorrect. The esophagus does not rely on a lack of air.

choices.text: The action of swallowing is strong enough to propel food to the gut in one movement
choices.explanation: Incorrect. A single swallow does not push food all the way; peristalsis carries it.

questions.explanation:
The answer is peristalsis in the esophageal wall. Peristalsis is a wave of muscle contraction that pushes food along the esophagus.

Because these muscle waves squeeze the food forward, they work even against gravity, so you can swallow while upside down. Gravity helps a little when you are upright, but it is not what moves the food.

Big idea: peristalsis, not gravity, moves food through the digestive tract.

questions.prompt: All of the following are regions of the stomach with the exception of the:

choices.explanation: Incorrect. The cardia is the region around the opening from the esophagus.
Incorrect. The fundic region is the dome at the top.
Incorrect. The body is the large middle region.
Incorrect. The pyloric part leads to the small intestine.
Correct. A ventricle is part of the heart, not the stomach.

questions.explanation:
The answer is the ventricle. The regions of the stomach are the cardia, fundus, body, and pyloric part.

'Ventricle' is the name for a chamber of the heart (or of the brain), not a part of the stomach.

Big idea: the stomach's four regions are cardia, fundus, body, and pylorus.

questions.prompt: Cells responsible for the regrowth of lost gut cells are known as:

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Mucous cells make mucus.
Correct. Stem cells divide to replace lost gut cells.
Incorrect. Parietal cells make acid.
Incorrect. Chief cells make pepsinogen.
Incorrect. Neither mucous nor parietal cells regrow the lining.

questions.explanation:
The answer is stem cells. The lining of the stomach and intestines is replaced every few days because acid, enzymes, and food constantly wear it down.

Stem cells at the base of the gastric pits and intestinal crypts divide to make new lining cells. Mucous cells, parietal cells, and chief cells have other specific jobs.

Big idea: the gut lining renews itself quickly thanks to stem cells.

questions.prompt: Lake is experiencing significant distress over dropping his phone down 5 flights of stairs. Which phase of gastric secretion does this exemplify, and what is the resulting effect on stomach secretory effect?

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Stress decreases secretion; it does not increase it.
Incorrect. Stress decreases gastric secretion.
Correct. Emotional upset inhibits gastric secretion in the gastric phase.
Incorrect. Stress decreases, not increases, secretion.
Incorrect. The key places this effect in the gastric phase.

questions.explanation:
The key's answer is the gastric phase, with decreased secretion. Strong emotions like distress or anger activate the sympathetic nervous system.

Many textbooks (such as Marieb) list emotional upset as an inhibitor of stomach secretion during the gastric phase, because sympathetic signals override the parasympathetic signals that normally boost acid production. So Lake's stress decreases stomach secretions.

Big idea: stress and fear slow digestion.

questions.prompt: What compound is necessary for conversion of pepsin to pepsinogen?

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Intrinsic factor helps absorb vitamin B12.
Incorrect. 'Gastric factor' is not the activator.
Incorrect. Mucus protects the stomach lining.
Correct. HCl converts pepsinogen into active pepsin.
Incorrect. Bile salts work in the small intestine on fats.

questions.explanation:
The answer is hydrochloric acid (HCl). The question's wording is reversed: it is pepsinogen that gets converted into pepsin, not the other way around.

Chief cells release pepsinogen, an inactive enzyme. Hydrochloric acid from parietal cells cuts off part of pepsinogen, turning it into active pepsin, which digests protein. Pepsin then helps activate more pepsinogen.

Big idea: stomach acid activates the protein-digesting enzyme pepsin.

questions.prompt: Hank eats 20 pieces of sushi. The activation of gut stretch receptors from this meal results in all of the following effects except for:

choices.explanation: Correct. Acetylcholine here comes from parasympathetic nerves, not sympathetic ones.
Incorrect. Stretching increases gastric juice secretion.
Incorrect. Stretching increases HCl secretion.
Incorrect. Stretching causes gastrin release.
Incorrect. Stretching leads to pepsin activation (the wording is reversed).

questions.explanation:
The answer is 'sympathetic release of acetylcholine'. When food stretches the stomach, stretch receptors trigger local reflexes and parasympathetic (vagus nerve) reflexes that release acetylcholine.

This increases gastric juice, HCl, and gastrin, and leads to activation of pepsinogen into pepsin (choice E's wording is reversed). The sympathetic system does not do this, so A is the exception.

Big idea: food stretching the stomach turns on digestion through parasympathetic reflexes.

questions.prompt: Food exiting the stomach first enters the:

choices.explanation: Incorrect. The ilium is a hip bone (the intestine is the 'ileum', and it comes last).
Incorrect. The ischium is a hip bone.
Correct. Food enters the duodenum after leaving the stomach.
Incorrect. The jejunum comes after the duodenum.
Incorrect. The pylorus is the last part of the stomach itself.

questions.explanation:
The answer is the duodenum. Food leaving the stomach passes through the pyloric sphincter into the duodenum, the first part of the small intestine.

The ilium and ischium are hip bones (not to be confused with the ileum, the last part of the small intestine). The pylorus is part of the stomach.

Big idea: stomach, then duodenum, jejunum, and ileum.

questions.prompt: The ilium includes a large concentration of lymphatic mucosa-associated lymphoid tissues which prevent entrance of bacteria into the bloodstream. Patches of these tissues are referred to as:

choices.explanation: Incorrect. 'Autoimmune clusters' is not a real structure.
Incorrect. 'Phagocytosis bunches' is not a real structure.
Incorrect. 'Lymphatic groups' is not the name.
Correct. Peyer's patches are lymphoid tissue in the ileum.
Incorrect. The specific name is Peyer's patches.

questions.explanation:
The answer is Peyer's patches. Peyer's patches are clusters of lymphoid tissue in the wall of the ileum (spelled 'ilium' in the question).

They are part of MALT (mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue). They sample germs from the intestine and start immune responses, helping keep bacteria from entering the blood.

Big idea: the gut has its own immune tissue because food carries germs.

questions.prompt: Which of the following structures is not a part of the large intestine?

choices.explanation: Incorrect. The cecum is part of the large intestine.
Incorrect. The appendix is attached to the large intestine.
Incorrect. The rectum is part of the large intestine.
Incorrect. The colon is the main part of the large intestine.

choices.text: All of the above are regions of the large intestine
choices.explanation: Correct. All of these are parts of the large intestine.

questions.explanation:
The answer is 'All of the above are regions of the large intestine'. The large intestine includes the cecum, the appendix (attached to the cecum), the colon, the rectum, and the anal canal.

So none of the listed structures is outside the large intestine.

Big idea: the large intestine runs from the cecum to the anus.

questions.prompt: Serotonin
questions.context: Match the following descriptions with their corresponding enteroendocrine cell secretions. A. Stimulates intestinal motility and HCl secretion B. Increases gastric motility and inhibits acid secretion C. Increases HCl secretion alone D. Inhibits gastric and pancreatic secretions and motility, as well as reduces blood circulation in the small intestine E. Modulating effects that affect short- and long-term energy balance

choices.explanation: Incorrect. A = stimulates intestinal motility and HCl secretion (gastrin).
Correct. B = increases gastric motility and inhibits acid secretion (serotonin).
Incorrect. C = increases HCl secretion alone (histamine).
Incorrect. D = inhibits gastric and pancreatic secretions and motility (somatostatin).
Incorrect. E = affects short- and long-term energy balance (gut-brain peptides).

questions.note: The original list was lettered A, B, C, E, F (no D); it is relabelled A-E here so the letters match the answer choices and the key.
questions.explanation:
The answer is B. In the stomach and intestine, serotonin is released by enterochromaffin cells. It increases the muscle contractions of the gut and is matched here with 'increases gastric motility and inhibits acid secretion'.

Big idea: the gut makes most of the body's serotonin, which helps control gut movement.

questions.prompt: Histamine
questions.context: Match the following descriptions with their corresponding enteroendocrine cell secretions. A. Stimulates intestinal motility and HCl secretion B. Increases gastric motility and inhibits acid secretion C. Increases HCl secretion alone D. Inhibits gastric and pancreatic secretions and motility, as well as reduces blood circulation in the small intestine E. Modulating effects that affect short- and long-term energy balance

choices.explanation: Incorrect. A = stimulates intestinal motility and HCl secretion (gastrin).
Incorrect. B = increases gastric motility and inhibits acid secretion (serotonin).
Correct. C = increases HCl secretion alone (histamine).
Incorrect. D = inhibits gastric and pancreatic secretions and motility (somatostatin).
Incorrect. E = affects short- and long-term energy balance (gut-brain peptides).

questions.note: The original list was lettered A, B, C, E, F (no D); it is relabelled A-E here so the letters match the answer choices and the key.
questions.explanation:
The answer is C. Histamine is released by enterochromaffin-like cells in the stomach. It acts directly on parietal cells to increase hydrochloric acid secretion.

Big idea: histamine is a strong acid signal, which is why some acid-reducing drugs block histamine.

questions.prompt: Gastrin
questions.context: Match the following descriptions with their corresponding enteroendocrine cell secretions. A. Stimulates intestinal motility and HCl secretion B. Increases gastric motility and inhibits acid secretion C. Increases HCl secretion alone D. Inhibits gastric and pancreatic secretions and motility, as well as reduces blood circulation in the small intestine E. Modulating effects that affect short- and long-term energy balance

choices.explanation: Correct. A = stimulates intestinal motility and HCl secretion (gastrin).
Incorrect. B = increases gastric motility and inhibits acid secretion (serotonin).
Incorrect. C = increases HCl secretion alone (histamine).
Incorrect. D = inhibits gastric and pancreatic secretions and motility (somatostatin).
Incorrect. E = affects short- and long-term energy balance (gut-brain peptides).

questions.note: The original list was lettered A, B, C, E, F (no D); it is relabelled A-E here so the letters match the answer choices and the key.
questions.explanation:
The answer is A. Gastrin is made by G cells. It increases HCl secretion and also stimulates gut motility, matching 'stimulates intestinal motility and HCl secretion'.

Big idea: gastrin is the main hormone that turns on stomach acid.

questions.prompt: Gut-brain peptides
questions.context: Match the following descriptions with their corresponding enteroendocrine cell secretions. A. Stimulates intestinal motility and HCl secretion B. Increases gastric motility and inhibits acid secretion C. Increases HCl secretion alone D. Inhibits gastric and pancreatic secretions and motility, as well as reduces blood circulation in the small intestine E. Modulating effects that affect short- and long-term energy balance

choices.explanation: Incorrect. A = stimulates intestinal motility and HCl secretion (gastrin).
Incorrect. B = increases gastric motility and inhibits acid secretion (serotonin).
Incorrect. C = increases HCl secretion alone (histamine).
Incorrect. D = inhibits gastric and pancreatic secretions and motility (somatostatin).
Correct. E = affects short- and long-term energy balance (gut-brain peptides).

questions.note: The original list was lettered A, B, C, E, F (no D); it is relabelled A-E here so the letters match the answer choices and the key.
questions.explanation:
The answer is E. Gut-brain peptides (such as ghrelin, PYY, and GLP-1) carry messages between the gut and brain about hunger and fullness, affecting short- and long-term energy balance.

Big idea: the gut helps control appetite by signaling the brain. (The original list used E and F; it is relabeled D and E here.)

questions.prompt: Somatostatin
questions.context: Match the following descriptions with their corresponding enteroendocrine cell secretions. A. Stimulates intestinal motility and HCl secretion B. Increases gastric motility and inhibits acid secretion C. Increases HCl secretion alone D. Inhibits gastric and pancreatic secretions and motility, as well as reduces blood circulation in the small intestine E. Modulating effects that affect short- and long-term energy balance

choices.explanation: Incorrect. A = stimulates intestinal motility and HCl secretion (gastrin).
Incorrect. B = increases gastric motility and inhibits acid secretion (serotonin).
Incorrect. C = increases HCl secretion alone (histamine).
Correct. D = inhibits gastric and pancreatic secretions and motility (somatostatin).
Incorrect. E = affects short- and long-term energy balance (gut-brain peptides).

questions.note: The original list was lettered A, B, C, E, F (no D); it is relabelled A-E here so the letters match the answer choices and the key.
questions.explanation:
The answer is D. Somatostatin is made by D cells. It is a general 'brake' that inhibits stomach and pancreatic secretions and slows gut movement.

Big idea: somatostatin turns digestion down, balancing gastrin and other 'go' signals.

questions.prompt: Jared has difficulty reading his diagnosis, so you read it for him. He most likely has a case of:
questions.context: Jared, 19, presents with a 4-day history of sharp and constant pain centered around his right iliac fossa. This pain is worsened by movement, but presented with no urinary or bowel difficulties. A blood test reveals slightly elevated WBC levels, and a urine test finds no abnormalities. He does not show signs of fever, and complains that he is hungry.

choices.explanation: Incorrect. He has no bowel problems, so diarrhea is unlikely.
Incorrect. Duodenal ulcer pain is in the upper abdomen.
Incorrect. Lactose intolerance causes cramping after dairy, not constant lower-right pain.
Incorrect. Hepatitis causes upper-right pain and jaundice.
Correct. Lower-right pain and high white cells point to appendicitis.

questions.explanation:
The answer is appendicitis. Jared has sharp, constant pain in the right iliac fossa (the lower right part of the abdomen), which is where the appendix is.

The pain gets worse with movement, his white blood cells are slightly high (a sign of infection), and his urine is normal (ruling out kidney or bladder problems). These all fit appendicitis. Being hungry and having no fever are less typical, but do not rule it out.

Big idea: the location of abdominal pain helps identify the affected organ.

questions.prompt: Select all of the symptoms which support your answer above.
questions.context: Jared, 19, presents with a 4-day history of sharp and constant pain centered around his right iliac fossa. This pain is worsened by movement, but presented with no urinary or bowel difficulties. A blood test reveals slightly elevated WBC levels, and a urine test finds no abnormalities. He does not show signs of fever, and complains that he is hungry.

choices.text: “Pain centered around his right iliac fossa”
choices.explanation: Correct. Pain in the right iliac fossa is the classic appendicitis location.
Correct. High white blood cells suggest infection or inflammation.
Correct. A normal urine test rules out urinary causes of the pain.

choices.text: “He does not show signs of fever”
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Appendicitis often causes a low fever, so no fever does not support it.
Incorrect. Appendicitis usually causes loss of appetite, so hunger does not support it.

questions.explanation:
The answers are A, B, and C. Pain centered in the right iliac fossa is the classic location of appendicitis. Slightly high white blood cells show the body is fighting an infection or inflammation.

A normal urine test helps rule out other causes of lower abdominal pain, like a kidney stone or urinary infection. Having no fever and feeling hungry do not support appendicitis; people with appendicitis often have a low fever and lose their appetite.

Big idea: doctors use multiple clues together to make a diagnosis.

questions.prompt: Ralph’s most likely diagnosis is:
questions.context: Ralph is a 56-year-old man who presents with abdominal pain and swelling as well as jaundice. He is a big fan of cycling and lives in the countryside. He also drinks regularly, and has been losing weight over the past 3 months. A blood test finds he has high urea levels and normal sodium levels.

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Stomach cancer does not usually cause jaundice.
Correct. Jaundice, swelling, drinking, and weight loss point to liver cancer.
Incorrect. Pancreatic cancer can cause jaundice, but his drinking history and swelling fit liver cancer better.
Incorrect. Esophageal cancer causes trouble swallowing, not jaundice.
Incorrect. Appendicitis causes sudden lower-right pain, not jaundice.

questions.explanation:
The answer is liver cancer. Ralph has abdominal pain and swelling, jaundice (yellowing from bilirubin buildup), regular drinking, and weight loss over months.

Heavy drinking damages the liver over time, raising the risk of cirrhosis and liver cancer. Jaundice points to a liver problem, and weight loss is common with cancer. Abdominal swelling can come from fluid buildup due to liver disease.

Big idea: cancers of the digestive system have warning signs, and alcohol is a major risk factor for liver cancer.

questions.prompt: True/false: a MRI can help confirm Ralph’s diagnosis.
questions.context: Ralph is a 56-year-old man who presents with abdominal pain and swelling as well as jaundice. He is a big fan of cycling and lives in the countryside. He also drinks regularly, and has been losing weight over the past 3 months. A blood test finds he has high urea levels and normal sodium levels.
questions.explanation:
This statement is true. An MRI uses magnets and radio waves to make detailed pictures of soft tissues like the liver.

Doctors use MRI (and CT scans) to see liver tumors and help confirm a diagnosis of liver cancer, often along with blood tests and sometimes a biopsy.

Big idea: imaging helps doctors diagnose digestive system cancers.

questions.prompt: Which of the following are risk factors for Ralph’s diagnosis? (Select all that apply)
questions.context: Ralph is a 56-year-old man who presents with abdominal pain and swelling as well as jaundice. He is a big fan of cycling and lives in the countryside. He also drinks regularly, and has been losing weight over the past 3 months. A blood test finds he has high urea levels and normal sodium levels.

choices.explanation: Correct. Liver cancer is more common in men.
Correct. The risk of liver cancer rises with age.
Incorrect. Cycling is not a risk factor for liver cancer.
Incorrect. Living in the countryside is not a known risk factor.
Correct. Heavy alcohol use is a major risk factor for liver cancer.

questions.explanation:
The answers are male, older age, and drinking alcohol. Liver cancer is more common in men, becomes more common with age, and is strongly linked to heavy alcohol use, which scars the liver.

Cycling and living in the countryside are not known risk factors.

Big idea: knowing risk factors helps prevent cancers of the digestive system.

questions.prompt: Only some breakdown products derived from _______ are absorbed through the lacteals of villi.

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Carbohydrate breakdown products enter blood capillaries.
Incorrect. Protein breakdown products enter blood capillaries.
Correct. Lipid products enter the lacteals.
Incorrect. Amino acids enter blood capillaries.

questions.explanation:
The answer is lipids. After fats are digested, the fatty acids and monoglycerides are packed into chylomicrons inside intestinal cells.

Chylomicrons are too large to enter blood capillaries, so they enter the lacteals, the lymph vessels in each villus. Sugars and amino acids go directly into the blood capillaries instead.

Big idea: absorbed fats travel through the lymphatic system before reaching the blood.

questions.prompt: Which is false in regards to the small intestine?

choices.text: It begins at the pyloric sphincter.
choices.explanation: Incorrect (this is true). The small intestine starts at the pyloric sphincter.

choices.text: The hepatopancreatic sphincter (sphincter of Oddi) regulates the flow of both bile and pancreatic juice from the ampulla into the jejunum.
choices.explanation: Correct (this is false). The sphincter of Oddi releases into the duodenum, not the jejunum.

choices.text: The jejunum is about 0.9 meters long.
choices.explanation: Incorrect (this is treated as true). The jejunum is roughly a meter or more long.

choices.text: The ileum is the longest portion and ends at the ileocecal sphincter.
choices.explanation: Incorrect (this is true). The ileum is the longest part and ends at the ileocecal sphincter.

questions.explanation:
The false statement is B. The sphincter of Oddi controls the flow of bile and pancreatic juice from the ampulla into the duodenum, not the jejunum.

The other statements are true: the small intestine begins at the pyloric sphincter, the jejunum is roughly a meter or more long (estimates vary), and the ileum is the longest part and ends at the ileocecal sphincter.

Big idea: bile and pancreatic juice enter the duodenum, the first part of the small intestine.

questions.prompt: _______ are deep ridges in the mucosa and submucosa that facilitate absorption. These occur near the proximal part of the duodenum and ending near the middle of the ileum.

choices.explanation: Correct. Circular folds are deep ridges of the mucosa and submucosa.
Incorrect. Villi are mucosa-only projections, smaller than circular folds.
Incorrect. Microvilli are tiny projections on individual cells.
Incorrect. Intestinal glands are pits that make secretions.

questions.explanation:
The answer is circular folds (plicae circulares). These are deep, permanent ridges of the mucosa and submucosa that circle the inside of the small intestine.

They slow food down and spin it, giving more time and surface for absorption. Villi are smaller finger-like projections on the folds, microvilli are tiny projections on each cell, and intestinal glands are pits between villi.

Big idea: folds, villi, and microvilli all increase the small intestine's surface area.

questions.prompt: Vitamin B12 is unique among water-soluble vitamins in that it requires intrinsic factor to be absorbed in the gut. In a disease called pernicious anemia, patients lack intrinsic factor and thus cannot absorb vitamin B12. Vitamin B12 is primarily absorbed in which portion of the GI tract?

choices.explanation: Incorrect. The duodenum absorbs iron and some other nutrients, not B12.
Incorrect. The jejunum (spelled 'jejunom' here) absorbs most nutrients, but not B12.
Correct. Vitamin B12 is absorbed in the ileum.
Incorrect. The colon mainly absorbs water.

questions.explanation:
The answer is the ileum. Vitamin B12 must be attached to intrinsic factor (made by the stomach's parietal cells) to be absorbed.

The B12-intrinsic factor pair is absorbed by special receptors found only in the ileum, the last part of the small intestine. If the ileum is removed or damaged, B12 cannot be absorbed.

Big idea: different nutrients are absorbed in different parts of the gut.

questions.prompt: All of the following are associated with duodenal ulcers except:

choices.explanation: Correct. Caffeine is not a recognized cause of duodenal ulcers.
Incorrect. NSAIDs are a major cause of ulcers.
Incorrect. Severe burns can cause stress ulcers in the duodenum.
